\CRcharacter*{Mira Silt}{the aunt who knows and will not say}{build/art/characters/mira-silt.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Mira, Mira of the Fishstairs, Dessa’s sister}\CRfield{Role}{family}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 785, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; returned thin)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; House Silt}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Fishstairs, Sill; eel trade; House Silt}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twenty-seven, broad-hipped, with eel slime dried on her sleeves and a small smile she keeps on her face the way another woman keeps a door on the latch: it can be shut without anybody noticing the movement. The top half of her left ear is missing, taken by a knife in a Fishstairs quarrel when she was nineteen; she says a hook did it, and the scar says otherwise, and nobody has ever made anything of it. She smells of river silt, salted perch, tallow smoke and the cold off the water. She carries a string of eel-bones in her pocket and flicks them against her thumb when she is deciding whether to lie, which is often. The thing people notice first is the smile; the thing they notice last is that she never sits down at a table where a slate is open.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Fast, low, with the proverb turned sideways. She answers a question with a question and then answers it herself, which gives her the room to choose which answer the listener gets. She never tells a story with a beginning; she starts at the part where somebody is already in trouble. She has learned from Fen traders to mark accounts in knots rather than on slate, and will not write a name down if a knot will hold it. When she is being kind she becomes brisk, because kindness in her house is a thing done quickly before anyone can make a speech about it.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “You want to know. You don’t want to know. I can see which one’s winning.”

\item “The secret’s in what happens to it after. I didn’t tell anybody anything. There’s nothing to tell. That’s the whole of it.”

\item “It came from a warm house, that’s all. There’s barley in it and a little smoke and it’s a crust, not a sermon.”

\item “Nineteen steps. Your sister counts them. I count the ones she doesn’t take.”

\item “Don’t ask a Fishstairs woman what she saw. She’ll sell it to you and then it’s yours and you’ll have to carry it.”

\item “He’s warm. That’s all I’ll say on a slate, and I’m saying it off the slate.”

\item “I kept your secret for three years, Dessa. Don’t make it a fourth.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
Born in Low Kiln to the same thin-returned mother as Dessa, Mira learned the eel trade at the Fishstairs at twelve and has worked the dawn market there ever since. She knows which households pay and which owe, which collectors take their ale before a collection and which after, and which boats on the Ilm are carrying something other than fish. She has been the district’s informal ledger of who is warm and who is cooling for fifteen years, and has never once put a name on paper.

She was in the room on Stone 7, Y.H. 812, when her sister bore the child with the branching red flower. She saw Sella Vail carry a covered bundle up the Clay Yard three days later, and she understood what had been done without being told. Alda Reed told Dessa the boy was among the Forty; Mira let her believe it. She has let her believe it for three years, and has taken a share of the barley Sella pays every winter, which she spends on Dessa, who does not know where the barley comes from. She has a child of her own, returned thin in Y.H. 802 to a household in Nine Pots, who does not recognize her; she has walked to Nine Pots twice and never knocked.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Her sister’s lie is hers too, and she has begun to feel the weight of it in the hand that holds the eel knife. She fears that telling Dessa the truth will put the boy on a slate that someone can use against him; she fears more that if she waits much longer the truth will come out in a quarrel, which is the worst way for a thing like that to be said. She fears she has become a woman who trades in other people’s warmth and calls it looking after them. Her contradiction: she gossips all day at the Fishstairs and has kept the one secret that matters for three years without a single slip.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants Dessa to stop reaching for a child she believes is dead, and she wants to be believed once about something that is not a rumour. She thinks she wants the truth to come out, and has arranged her life so that it never has to. What she needs is to understand that a secret kept out of love is still a debt, and that it gathers Ash like any other debt, and that the only way to stop paying interest on it is to say the thing.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Dessa Silt} — her sister, her room-mate, the woman whose child she has hidden for three years. Dessa suspects; Mira has begun to be afraid of the moment Dessa stops suspecting and knows. Everything between them is said in the language of barley, coughs and the nineteen steps. \emph{Ch 1:} she crossed the room and pressed a crust of Vail-smoked barley into Dessa’s hand in two brisk movements, stopping short of the slate to do it.

\textbf{Corin} — the nephew she watches from a distance at the market and once followed as far as the Clay Yard. She has never called him anything, not even in her head, because a name is a thing that can be overheard. \emph{Ch 1:} she would not hold him and would not sit where the slate lay open, but pushed the wool back under him briskly with two movements before anyone could make a speech about it. \emph{Ch 3:} a background figure at the eel stall in the afternoon, eel slime dried pale on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone; she flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and never once looked at the basket. When she turned to go she shoved a loose board clear of the barrow men’s path with the side of her hand, brisk, her face still toward the eels. She had not looked at him once all day. He put her not-looking beside the man on the block’s: one priced him, the other kept him, and he had no word in Grathic for either.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — they have an arrangement: barley and silence. Mira has begun to resent the barley and has never once refused it, which is the precise shape of her complicity. \emph{Ch 1:} she watched the hand in the door without moving, her thumb quiet in her pocket and the eel-bone put away.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — they trade small facts and never the large one. Alda knows more about the birth; Mira knows more about what happened after it. Neither will sit at a table with a slate on it, and they have built a friendship entirely out of things said standing up. \emph{Ch 1:} they worked the same room standing, each with her back to the writing.

\textbf{Orra Weir} — her supplier at the Weir and her oldest friend, who wants the secret out and has said so twice. Mira has answered both times with the weather.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — buys her eels for the levy feast and pays in marks that are short by two. She short-weights him by two eels. This small war has been going on for six years and neither has acknowledged it. \emph{Ch 3:} at the eel stall she asked him the price and answered it herself --- \emph{two marks the pair or two marks the pair and two short? Don’t trouble yourself. It’s two marks the pair and two short, and I’ve counted them twice, and I’ll count them again after I’ve eaten.} He did not answer, because she had left him nothing in the sentence that wanted an answer. She moved an eel-bone from hand to hand and said a figure under her breath. The knot-string is still not shown; only the counting is.

\textbf{Tarn} — the Vail’s clay-bound hand. She has suspected for a year that he is more than the debt he says he is, and has not asked, because she recognizes a person who keeps a secret and knows better than to open him.

\textbf{Ch 5.} At the Fishstairs on Stone 14 and the market’s edge on Stone 15 she worked with pale slime on her sleeves and silt in her neck, head held a little to the right against the cold where the ear had been. She flicked three eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and put one away when the deciding was done; she gave Berr four eels where six should go against his two marks short of six years, and neither acknowledged the war. Asked whose the basket was, she answered with a question and then her own: \emph{he’s warm} --- all she would say on a slate, and she was saying it off the slate. Her grey wool cord at the waist was touched three times in two mornings when a number was spoken, and the second cord twisted twice beneath it has never gone up the river to Nine Pots and has never been lifted at a door; the thumb goes always to the first. She put a brown-edged crust into the fold briskly, called it a crust and not a sermon, and went back to the eels without looking in.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 28 she came up the Clay Yard from the fish-trade with pale eel slime dried on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, head held to the right against the cold. Asked whose basket was going past, she answered with a question and her own answer --- \emph{Whose do you think? A basket’s a basket. It came from a warm house, that’s all, and it’s going back to one} --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and put it away. When a woman at the well said a figure for the Five, her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed there while she decided, and came out with another bone between finger and thumb. She crossed three paces and put a fresh brown-edged barley crust into the fold beside the spent one, saying \emph{It’s a crust, not a sermon}, and went back to the eels without looking in; the old crust lay stiff where it had lain since Stone 15 and neither woman named either. Shifting the basket’s weight showed the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, the one never taken upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door; the knots on neither were counted. Three doors down Dessa coughed from the pits and called it weather, and Mira’s smile did not move. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 8.} On the Last Day she came up from the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, brisk, answering a question with a question and her own answer --- a basket came from a warm house and goes back to one --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb before putting it away. When a figure was spoken her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided, and shifting the weight showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door; the knots were not counted. She put nothing into the fold this chapter --- no third crust came --- and went back down the yard without once looking in or saying she knew the child.

\textbf{Ch 9.} On Ilmen 2 she came up from the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves and silt in the hollow of her neck, head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, and answered a question about the eels with a question and her own answer. When a figure was spoken at the well her thumb went under her apron to the grey wool cord and stayed while she decided; shifting the basket showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, and neither was counted. On Ilmen 8 she came up again and passed her sister at the end of nineteen steps without looking at her, brought no crust and put nothing into the fold, and went back down the yard toward the eels without once looking in. Two not-lookings of the same shape were opposite things and the boy kept them apart. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 10.} She comes up from the eels at the brook’s edge on Ilmen 9 with pale slime dried on her sleeves and her head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, answers a neighbour’s question about the water with her own answer, brings no crust and does not look into the basket on the bank where her sister lies dead. At the Fishstairs on Ilmen 12 she answers a question about the run with a question and then her own --- \emph{It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- and shifting the weight of a basket shows the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted. On the river road on Ilmen 14 she tells Sella to ask Orra what night the boat came and not what she is owed, because Orra will tell her the oars; on Ilmen 15, at the blessing, she gives the same answer in the same form and keeps her grey wool on its own board beside Orra’s knot-string without letting the two touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and her small smile stays on the latch.

\textbf{Ch 11.} On Day 45 she worked the eels at the far racks with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been. Asked whether the run would come with the blessing done she answered the question and then her own --- \emph{Does it come now the stone’s blessed? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- and flicked an eel-bone against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. When a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and shifting a basket showed the second twisted twice beneath it, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, neither knot counted. Her board stood beside Orra’s and did not touch it. The smoky crust she put in the fold on Stone 28 is gone by the afternoon of Day 46, taken quietly and never named; the boy set her hand on a tray with two other hands and made no cause of it. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 12.} On Day 53 she answered a question about the run with a question and her own answer and moved eel-bones while deciding whether to lie; when a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed. The second cord twisted twice beneath it showed and was not carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, and her board lay beside Orra’s without touching it. Dessa has been dead sixteen mornings and she has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the barley and the silence between her and Sella went on unentered, as did the small war with Berr over two marks short and two eels short.

\textbf{Ch 13.} At the last market before Silt she worked the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been. Asked about the run she answered a question with a question and her own answer, and moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. A figure was spoken; her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed, and shifting a basket showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted. Her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket. Her not-looking was a keeping; the man at the block’s not-looking had been a pricing, and she had no word in Grathic for either. Dessa has been dead twenty-two mornings and she has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

\textbf{Ch 14.} On Silt 2 she worked the eels at the outer boards of the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, river silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on its face the way a door is kept on the latch. Asked whether the run would come now the month had turned, she answered the question and her own — \emph{Does it come now? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} — and moved eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding was done. When a buyer said a figure her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed, and shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own. Her board lay beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket; her not-looking was a keeping where Berr’s not-looking at the same shade was a pricing, and the boy set the two in places that did not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and Dessa is twenty-nine mornings dead.

\textbf{Ch 15.} On Silt 13, the day the water fell, she worked the eels at the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on the latch. A woman come down the steps with salt white at her wrists asked whether the run would be thin now the water had gone down; Mira flicked an eel-bone against her thumb, answered the question and her own --- \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- moved two bones hand to hand while deciding whether to lie and put one away when the deciding was done. A buyer in a wet coat named a figure; her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed while she decided, and shifting a creel showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver not touched. Her board stood beside Orra’s knot-string and did not touch it. She brought no crust and did not look into the basket; her not-looking was a keeping where the man at the block’s was a pricing, and the boy set the two in places that did not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, and Dessa is thirty-six mornings dead.

\textbf{Ch 16.} On Day 76, Silt 17, she works the eels below the north bridge at the Fishstairs with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been, the small smile kept on her face the way a door is kept on the latch. Asked whether the run will be thin she answers her own answer --- \emph{Thin? Who’s to say thin? It comes when it comes. Ask the river} --- moves eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and puts one away when the deciding is done. When a buyer names a figure she says \emph{Two marks the pair and two short --- you’ve said it twice and I’ve counted it twice ... there’s nothing in the sentence that wants an answer}, and her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays there while she decides. Shifting a creel shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots, never lifted at a door, neither knot counted by any thumb but her own and the knot for the thin child upriver untouched. Her board lies beside Orra Weir’s knot-string and does not touch it; Orra is present only as the board, not on stage. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket. The steps have come back four, four and a landing a hand’s breadth out of line that a whole market walks over carefully without making a fall of it, and the soft-cuffed clerk still sits for a measure nobody called, hand to slate before eyes to stalls; the boy files the order apart from Marra, the Drawing collector and the Court-table clerk, with no sixth sighting of the neat dark hand. Her not-speaking, her not-looking and Berr’s taking-himself-out-of-his-sentence stand as three omissions of one shape that do not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s, thirty-eight mornings dead now.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
She is in the birth room from the first hours of Day 1 and is already arranged: the smile kept on the face like a door on the latch, the back turned to the slate, the eel-bones flicked and put away. She says the one true thing in the room --- that the secret is in what happens to a child after it is born --- in a form that can be taken as nothing, and follows it with \emph{there’s nothing to tell}. In Chapter 3 she is seen for the first time in her own element, the eel stall at the Cross, and the arrangement holds: dried slime, the missing top of her left ear, a question asked and answered by herself, a board shoved clear for the barrow men, and not one look into the basket all afternoon. The knot-string and the barley account are still offstage; the woman who knows and will not say is not. Her marker is reconciled to Chapter 1: she is on stage here, not first seen at the Fishstairs in Chapter 5.

On Days 8 and 9 the woman who knows is seen in her own element for two mornings, and the keeping becomes a craft with tools: eel-bones moved while an answer is chosen, a cord touched when a figure is spoken, a second cord kept apart and never taken to the door it belongs to. The little war with Berr is given its exact arithmetic --- four eels for six, two marks short for six years --- and neither will name it. She answers the question about the basket without letting the sentence want a reply, and gives the warmth briskly before anyone can make a speech about it, which is how kindness is done in her house. The knot-string itself is still not shown plainly and the knots are not counted; what the boy sees is the hand, the movement and the difference between two cords, and he has no word for any of it.

On Days 15 through 24 the two records stand side by side in the fold and the yard. On Stone 28 she answers a question about the basket with a lie in the form of a proverb, touches the grey cord when a figure is spoken, and gives the boy a fresh crust briskly, the second warmth in the fold beside the spent one from Stone 15. Both are entered nowhere and neither is named; a gift done quickly is a gift no one can make a speech about. The separate cord twisted twice below the grey shows again as she shifts the basket, still unknotted by any hand but her own and still not taken to the thin child upriver. Dessa’s cough comes up from the pits three doors down and is called weather, and the sister who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile. The boy sees the hand and the twist and counts neither, and cannot thank either woman for the bread.

On the Last Day the woman who knows comes up from the eels for a question about a basket and gives the same answer in the same form --- a question, then her own answer, with room to choose which answer the listener gets. The grey cord is touched under the apron when a figure is spoken, the second cord twisted twice shows beneath it, and neither is counted or carried to the door it belongs to; the knot-string itself stays unshown. She puts no crust in the fold this chapter and the two already there are neither eaten nor named; three doors down the house is quiet and she says nothing about knowing the child. The smile stays on the latch, the eel-bone goes away, and the secret she keeps out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at.

On Days 31 through 37 the woman who knows comes up twice from the eels and keeps the knowing under the same small smile. On Ilmen 2 she answers a question with a question and her own answer, flicks an eel-bone, touches the grey cord under her apron when a figure is spoken and shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it with the knots uncounted; on Ilmen 8 she passes her sister at the end of nineteen steps without looking at her, brings no crust and says nothing. The smile stays on the latch. The secret she keeps out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at, and her sister goes on going thin three doors down and calling it weather.

On Days 38 through 44 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while her sister goes into the brook and stays there. On Ilmen 9 she came up from the eels with slime dried pale on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, answered a neighbour’s question about the water with a silence and her own answer, brought no crust and did not look into the basket held on the bank above her sister’s body. On Ilmen 12 she came up from the eels at the Fishstairs, answered a question about the run with \emph{Does it come when you bless it? It comes when it comes. Ask the river}, flicked an eel-bone and put it away; when a figure was spoken her thumb went under her apron to the grey cord and stayed, and shifting the basket showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never carried upriver to Nine Pots and never lifted at a door, neither knot counted. She brought no third crust and did not look in. On Ilmen 14 she met Sella on the river road with eel-bones at her hip and said \emph{Ask her what night the boat came. Don’t ask her what she’s owed. She’ll tell you the oars.} On Ilmen 15 she answered a weir woman about the blessing with a question and her own answer, kept the grey cord and the second cord side by side with the knots uncounted, put her board beside Orra’s knot-string without letting the two touch, and did not look into the boy’s basket. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s.

On Days 45 through 47 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the record she keeps in wool stands beside another woman’s on a board that does not touch it. On Day 45 she answers a weir woman about the run with a question and her own answer, moves eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, touches the grey cord when a figure is spoken and shows the second twisted twice beneath it with neither knot counted. The smoky crust she gave on Stone 28 --- the warmth the boy most wanted and could never reach --- goes quietly out of the fold on Day 46 and nobody says it is gone, who took it or what became of it. The boy sets her hand on a tray with Sella’s and Alda’s and refuses to make a cause, and she is offstage for the rest of the chapter. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at.

On Days 48 through 54 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the record she keeps in wool stands beside another woman’s on a board that does not touch it. On Day 53 at the Fishstairs she works the eels with pale slime dried on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been; she answers a question about the run with a question and her own answer and flicks eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie, putting one away when the deciding is done. When a buyer says a figure her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays there while she decides, and shifting a basket shows the second cord twisted twice beneath the grey, never carried upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own. Her board lies beside Orra’s knot-string and does not touch it; the shape of the forty-first knot is legible to the boy without its name and the word is not spoken. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at.

On Days 55 through 60 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the month of mud arrives and the river begins to move. On Ilmen 30, the last Account-day and market before Silt, she works the eels at the Fishstairs with pale slime dried pale on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the top of her left ear had been. She answers a question about the run with a question and her own answer, moves eel-bones against her thumb while deciding whether to lie and puts one away when the deciding is done. When a figure is spoken her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays; shifting a basket shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never taken upriver to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knots on neither counted by any thumb but her own. Her board lies beside Orra’s knot-string and does not touch it, the shape of the forty-first knot legible without its name and the word unspoken. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket; her not-looking is a keeping where the man at the block’s is a pricing, and she has no Grathic word for either. Dessa is twenty-two mornings dead and uncollected and Mira has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at.

On Days 61 through 67 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the month turns toward mud and the river begins to come up. On Silt 2 she works the eels below the north bridge with pale slime on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the ear had been; she answers a question about the run with a question and her own answer, moves eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, and puts one away. When a buyer says a figure her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays, and the second cord twisted twice beneath it shows with neither knot counted, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door; her board stands beside Orra’s and does not touch it. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket. The boy sets her not-looking, a keeping, beside Berr’s not-looking, a pricing, and has no word in Grathic for either, and keeps them in two places that do not touch. She has not said she knows the child is Dessa’s; the secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at, and the woman it was kept from is twenty-nine mornings dead and uncollected.

On Days 68 through 74 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the river comes up and goes down. On Silt 13, as the water falls, she works the eels at the Fishstairs with pale slime on her sleeves, silt in the hollow of her neck and her head held right where the ear had been; she answers a question about the run with a question and her own answer, moves eel-bones while deciding whether to lie and puts one away, and when a buyer names a figure her thumb goes under her apron to the grey cord and stays while she decides. The second cord twisted twice beneath it shows with neither knot counted, never carried to Nine Pots or lifted at a door, the knot for the thin child upriver untouched, and her board lies beside Orra’s without touching it. She brings no crust and does not look into the basket; her not-looking is a keeping where Berr’s is a pricing, and the boy keeps them in places that do not touch. The secret kept out of love goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at, and the woman it was kept from is thirty-six mornings dead and uncollected.

On Days 75 through 77 the woman who knows keeps the knowing under the same small smile while the water goes out of the yard and the steps come back out of line. On Silt 17 she works the eels at the Fishstairs with slime dried on her sleeves, silt in her neck and her head held right where the ear had been; answers a question with her own answer and moves eel-bones while deciding whether to lie; puts her thumb to the grey cord when a buyer names a figure and shows the second cord twisted twice beneath it, never to Nine Pots or a door, neither knot counted and the thin child’s knot untouched. Her board lies beside Orra’s and does not touch it, she brings no crust and does not look into the basket. The kept secret goes on gathering interest in a record no Court’s thumb will look at, and the woman it was kept from is thirty-eight mornings dead and uncollected.

\item Ch 1: Came in from the yard with eel slime dried on her sleeves and the cold on them; stood in the one patch of floor the slate did not reach, back to the writing and face to the door. Answered a question with a question and then her own answer: the secret is in what happens to a child after. Said she had told nobody and there was nothing to tell. Flicked an eel-bone against her thumb and put it away when the hand came; kept the small smile on the latch all night. Crossed the room to press a crust of brown-edged Vail-smoked barley bread into Dessa’s hand, briskly, stopping short of the slate. The top of her left ear is missing --- a hook, she says; the scar says a knife.

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. Background figure at the eel stall at the edge of the Cross in the afternoon, with the top of her left ear gone and eel slime dried pale on her sleeves; kept her head a little to the right against the cold in the place where the ear had been. Flicked eel-bones against her thumb, asked Berr the eel price and answered it herself with \emph{two marks the pair and two short}, said a figure under her breath and moved another bone. Shoved a loose board clear of the barrow men’s path with the side of her hand and went on talking as if she had moved nothing. Never looked at the basket once all day.

Answered a question about the basket with a question and her own answer --- \emph{he’s warm}, off the slate --- and shifted her back to the corner of his open slate rather than look at it. \CRcharacter*{Sella Vail}{the woman who keeps the fire and asks no questions}{build/art/characters/sella-vail.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Sella, the Vail widow, Widow Vail, the keeper of the fire}\CRfield{Role}{family}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 779, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; born to a family of slip-mixers}\CRfield{Allegiance}{House Vail kiln-house, Clay Yard, Low Kiln; Kiln-Masters of Sill by widow’s mark}\CRfield{Status}{alive}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
A broad woman of thirty-three with forearms the colour of dried slip and a burn across the back of her left hand shaped like a little door --- two straight sides, a lintel and a threshold, the skin inside it puckered and pale --- which she keeps half-closed when she carries a cup, and which closes on nothing when her hand has nothing to hold. She is not tall and she does not make herself tall; she takes up room by being impossible to move. Her hair is coal-black with one grey streak at the temple that she says came from the winter Garl died and will not discuss further. She smells of woodsmoke, wet wool, and under it the faint sour mineral tang of the Ash ridge along the skirting board, which she has not swept in two years and does not intend to sweep. Her hands are never still. When they have nothing to do they count: spoons, nails, the breaths of a sleeping child. She wears her widow’s mark on a cord at her throat, a thumb-length of lead-glazed clay with the Vail kiln scratched into it, and she touches it before she opens the kiln and never at any other time. People notice the burn first and the mark last, which is the order she prefers.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Grathic proverbs and half-sentences, practical instruction addressed to the pot or the fire before it is addressed to a person. She says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and \emph{the boy} where another would say \emph{my son}. She never finishes a sentence that would require her to say what she feels, and she is not unaware of this; she has simply decided that a thing said aloud becomes a thing the Court can enter. Her humour is dry and costs her something. When she is angry she gets quieter, and the quieter she gets the more the household straightens up.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The fire doesn’t know you’re sorry. Feed it.”

\item “Don’t set that near the door. You’ll pay for it in the thaw.”

\item “He’s a boy. He’s warm. That’s the whole of what I know.”

\item “You can ask me what you like. I won’t answer it. Ask the pot instead; it’s more use.”

\item “A slate-name with no house is a coat anybody can wear. I’ve seen it before.”

\item “The boy comes under the roof on the morrow. The house will keep him.” --- the taking announced without an \emph{I} in it, and never explained.

\item “Don’t set that near the door. You’ll pay for it in the thaw.” --- instruction to the pot, not to a person, given with the kiln already open.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born in Low Kiln to slip-mixers, married Garl Vail at seventeen, and kept the Vail fire ever since in the way a widow keeps a wound clean: daily, without comment, with a hand that knows exactly how much pressure the thing will bear. She bore two children. Jorra, who lived, and Enna, who died at nine months of the second chill in Y.H. 804, after Alda Reed had warmed the stone and done everything the craft knew. Sella sat up with that child for three nights and learned what the midwives already knew: that a vessel can cool while everybody is being kind to it. In Y.H. 811, in the Long Cold, Garl died with the river iced and no collector able to cross, and his warmth went where unkept warmth goes. The Ash in the Vail corner is thicker than in any other house in the district. Sella has never swept it and has never said why.

On Stone 7, Y.H. 812, a woman in the district bore a child with a branching red flower across his ribs, and Sella took him in on the third day. She gave as her reason the one she has given ever since: a foundling with no house-name can be used by anyone, and a boy entered under a roof is a boy nobody can take for a levy without answering to that roof. This is true. It is not the whole of it. Alda Reed, who delivered him, crossed herself at the birth-flower and told nobody what she had seen, and Sella, who saw the same look on the midwife’s face, asked her nothing at all. She has kept the boy close for three years and has never once asked where his memory came from. She is waiting to see what he will become.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Enna’s second chill; Garl going uncollected; the Ash ridge that has grown an inch since. She fears another Long Cold, and fears more than that the day somebody from Slate Row notices that one child in her house listens to the fire before he looks at it. She fears Jorra, who has begun to disappear into the back rooms with men whose names are not spoken, and she fears that she has already lost the wheel to him while he still stands at it. Her contradiction is the whole of her: the woman who feeds every hungry child in the yard has never once said she loves one. She would sooner swallow the widow’s mark.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the fire to hold, the wheel to stay in the house, and a Vail name written on the birth-slate of every child born under her roof. She thinks she wants a whole return for Garl, so that he might come back as himself and sit where he used to sit and say nothing in his own voice. What she needs is to admit that she did not take Corin in for the house at all. She took him because he was the only warm thing in a room full of people pretending not to be cold, and because she had already lost one child to the second chill and could not bear to lose another to an explanation.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Jorra Vail} — her son, the keeper of the wheel. He believes she took the foundling in to replace Enna and to keep the house’s standing while he did the work. She has never told him otherwise, which is how he has come to believe it. They speak about the kiln, the levy, the weather; they do not speak about Garl, or Enna, or the boy. \emph{Ch 2:} he said \emph{he’s not Vail} when she announced the taking, and she did not answer him; she grew quieter and the house straightened up around it. He went on turning the wheel without looking at her and obeyed her before she had finished. The sentence stands and the boy is under the roof and still unwritten.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling she took in and has never questioned. She watches him with a hearth-maid’s attention and a widow’s refusal to name what she sees. Her silence is its own kind of Court: kindness that does not want an answer, and that therefore cannot be refused. \emph{Ch 1:} her hand came in ahead of her, felt for the heat at his belly, found none, opened and shut once over the covered bundle, and withdrew. She did not look at him, or at any of the women, and said nothing. \emph{Ch 2:} the hand that hovered now takes. She crossed to the bench first and put her hand near the slate as near a sleeping animal, then lifted him, the little-door burn closing first on nothing and then on his weight. She said \emph{the boy} and \emph{the house}, carried him up the yard without looking back, laid him on fresh straw, and gave instruction to the pot and the fire. She has not written him as Vail and has said nothing of payment or purpose. \emph{Ch 3:} she carried him out under the Vail roof for the first time, in a basket under a fold of wool, like a pot filled that must not be slopped. She kept a half-pace from every open slate, put the fold back without looking, answered a question about whose house with \emph{the house}, and answered a question about the mother with \emph{Account-day}. All morning she spoke to the wool and the wind: \emph{Keep it off his ears. It’s the river wind.} She did not look into the basket on the walk home and said nothing of what had been read over him.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — delivered Enna and Corin both, and crossed herself at the second birth. They have traded one silence for three years. Alda has the fuller notes; Sella has the fuller knowledge of what a silence costs when a household must eat. \emph{Ch 1:} Alda laid the slate flat on the bench as Sella’s hand went back out the door; the trade of silences begins in that room. \emph{Ch 2:} Sella put her hand near the writing on the bench as she took the child and did not touch it, and Alda did not look at her. The arrangement holds without a word passing between them.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — the woman who bore the boy. Sella knows it and has paid her in barley and slip-clay to stay away, and has never entered the payment in any account, not even the private one she keeps in her head. \emph{Ch 1:} Dessa’s pulse rose under her \emph{door shut} smile while the hand hung above her child; neither looked at the other. \emph{Ch 2:} Sella took the boy up the yard without once looking at the woman standing at the end of the nineteen steps, and Dessa did not follow.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — confirmed her widow’s mark and has never called in the debt Garl left against a shipment of tiles. The uncalled debt is worse than a called one, because she cannot pay it and cannot settle it and cannot stop owing it. \emph{Ch 3:} at the Slate Row end of the Cross he told her the mark was confirmed by the factor at Greybank, that it was a kindness, and that kindness is entered. She did not answer him about the mark; she pulled the wool up over the boy’s ear and said it was the river wind. He stood a moment with his mouth open on the next part, then left the debt where it lay as carefully as he had found it. She has never asked and has never thanked him, which he has decided means she knows.

\textbf{Garl Vail} — her husband, uncollected in the Long Cold. She decided he would not be collected; he did not ask her to decide. The Ash in the corner is the shape of that decision and she has lived beside it for a year. \emph{Ch 2:} she keeps his seat empty and his coat on its peg, will not let anyone sweep the ridge, and touches the widow’s mark only before she opens the kiln. The house keeps a roll of its own in which he is entered, and does not show it to a man from Slate Row.

\textbf{Ch 4.} The boy was carried to the Drawing and back like a pot filled that must not be slopped; she placed him where he could see and not join and stood a half-pace off, her burn shut on nothing, and would not be the one to tell him what the room was doing. She did not answer Jorra’s \emph{the back room’s cold}; she shifted the damper. With Alda, a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement, and neither asked what the other had written. Dessa at her threshold got no look from her and no word, and the barley between the two houses went on being unentered. Garl’s mark was touched before the kiln and not at the bank, and his coat, seat, ridge and proverb kept the house in his shape while the debt stayed uncalled.

\textbf{Ch 5.} The rule of the mark held exactly: touched before the opening on Stone 13 and at no other time, not at the bank that night or on Stone 15. She fed him barley gruel from the house’s own dish, holding his head with two fingers behind the ear, and gave every instruction to the fire, the pot and the wool --- \emph{keep it off his ears; it’s the river wind} --- never to the basket. She carried him down to the Fishstairs twice and to the market’s edge once, kept her half-pace from every open slate, laid marks for two pair of eels and counted them with her eyes, and said nothing about the collector’s cuff, the cord or where they had been. At dusk on Stone 15 her hand did not go to the mark; she counted loaves and bits with her lips and came back to the same place twice, keeping the shape of the days to Kindling without giving the number. She neither saw nor refused the crust Mira put in the fold, and where she is concerned these are the same thing.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 16 she touched the mark before the lid and at no other hour, moved her lips along the loaf shelf so the days to Kindling stood as a shape, and told the neighbour at the threshold to ask the pot. She carried him down to the Cross on Stone 20 and back, kept her half-pace from every open slate, set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and did not look into it; at dusk she put the fold right without his face, banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a reading is not an opening. On Stone 19 she slid the basket a hand’s breadth out of the draught and would not have called it love, measured the ridge with her thumb --- near two thumbs here, a finger more two doors down --- and said leave it until the Last Day. The crust Mira put in the fold went from warm to cold and she neither took it out nor named it. With Alda a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement again; Berr read his figure over the basket and went around Garl’s uncalled debt another year; Jorra moved the damper before she had finished and did not say the back room was cold.

\textbf{Ch 7.} Through Days 15--24 she went to the fire before anything else and touched the widow’s mark before each opening and at no other hour --- not when she banked with the back of a broken pot, not at the reading on Stone 30. She counted fuel and bread into the last tend in loaves, glances and the space where a loaf should have stood, and answered the man who came back from the ice with a number in his fist by saying it was a cold and feeding the fire. She sent Tarn for a collector for a neighbour, carried the basket two doors down and set it at the edge of the light with her burn shut on nothing. On Stone 29 she laid her thumb in the Vail Ash ridge and then in the death-house ridge, near two thumbs here and a finger thicker there, and walked back without saying which was which. At the last market she kept her half-pace from every open slate, set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and gave instruction to the wool, and at dusk put the fold right without looking at his face, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and banked the coals. She neither took out nor named either crust. With Alda a half-pace and a slate turned writing-down stood in for the arrangement again; she did not answer Jorra’s silence about the back room, let Berr go around Garl’s debt, and carried the keeping into Kindling without explaining any of it.

\textbf{Ch 8.} On Kindling she took the clay dish of fire up from the yard before first light, put her hand to the widow’s mark for one breath before she opened the kiln and tipped the coal in, and did not touch it again; nobody said where the flame came from or what it cost, and she gave the instruction to the fire and the wool and fed him from the house’s own dish, saying \emph{the house}. Through the Five the mark was touched before openings and at no other hour, never at the bank. At the Weighing she kept her half-pace from every open slate and did not repeat the name the officer read; the clean voice and the Court’s room reached the basket only as a sound through a doorway, and she did not turn toward it. On the Long Night she let the fire go out at dusk and sat with the others telling the Return in the dark, saying \emph{the house} where another woman would have said \emph{I} and going around Garl’s name as she went around Ash. On the Remembering she did not say Garl’s name and let Alda put dates where it should have stood. On the Last Day she would not let anyone sweep the Ash early, laid her thumb flat in the Vail ridge and then the neighbour’s, near two thumbs here and a finger’s width thicker two doors down, and left both where they lay. On Ilmen 1, with the grey burned in the morning and called dealt with by a neighbour and not by her, the coals were still banked under ash so there was no opening and she did not touch the mark; she put the fold right without looking at his face, fed him from the house’s own dish, and said nothing about where any of the warmth came from or who had paid for it.

\textbf{Ch 9.} Through Days 31–37 the keeping went on without an entry. At the well she drew with her free hand, the little-door burn closing on the rope and then on nothing, spoke \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and gave the instruction to the bucket, the fire and the wool and never to the basket; she did not say where the warmth in the household dish came from. On Ilmen 3 she fed him from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear and sat with the mark untouched at the bank, because a dusk is not an opening. On Ilmen 5 she stood a half-pace off while Alda laid dates and wrote what she turned down, and did not ask. On Ilmen 6 she touched the mark before the opening, held it one breath and let go, and did not touch it for a pot, a note or a nearly full sound. On Ilmen 8 she set him in the shade of the nineteen steps three doors down, carried him up the yard at dusk, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a bank was not an opening. She has said nothing about the payer of any warmth.

\textbf{Ch 10.} On Day 38 she holds the basket on the higher ground at the Slip Brook and turns the boy’s face toward the bank, as she would turn a pot so the light fell where she wanted it; she does not set him down. She goes to the fire, not down the road for a collector, and sends nobody; the omission is not entered and she does not name it. On Day 42 she fetches a clay jar from House Silt and sets it on the shelf by the wall, without turning the errand into a walk to a bank or opening a slate. On Day 43 and Day 44 she leaves the boy in shade at the Weir and carries him home at dusk, setting him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face. She still says \emph{the house}, gives every instruction to the wool, the fire and the pot, touches the mark only before openings, and has named neither the payer of the warmth nor the woman in the brook.

\textbf{Ch 11.} She carried him down to the Fishstairs before light and set him below the north bridge where a pot would be set, out of the draught, then up the Clay Yard and onto his bed at dusk, never into the Debt Loft; the fold went right at his ear without a look at his face. Every instruction went to the fire, the pot and the wool, and she said the house where another woman would have said I. She touched the widow’s mark once before the opening on Day 45 and not at any bank or on any other day. She fed him gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish, two fingers behind his ear, spoon wiped on her sleeve and his mouth not wiped. At the well she went at a half-pace from every open slate, went wide around a slate propped at the rack end and gave the instruction to the bucket. She said nothing about the payer of any warmth, did not name Dessa, and did not say that the smoky crust was gone. Her hand is one of the three the boy set on a tray as possible takers.

\textbf{Ch 12.} Through seven more days she gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and none to the basket, and said the house where another woman would say I. With Alda a half-pace and a turned slate stood in for the arrangement again while the fifth note went under a floorboard and she did not ask; with Berr the debt against the tiles lay where it lay and one in twelve went over the basket unchallenged; with Jorra the dust out of the back room went unasked about and the damper went ahead of her sentence. She did not look toward the bed or into the basket, did not touch the mark at a well or a bank, and said nothing about the payer of the milk, the coal that went up with the bird or the crust that went out of the fold on Day 46.

\textbf{Ch 13.} She carried him three doors down into House Silt on Ilmen 27 and set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and away from every open slate; she opened no slate and turned the errand into no walk to Slate Row. Alda came and she stood a half-pace off with her burn shut on nothing and asked no question about the birth-slates or the fold pressed too long. At the well and at the last market she gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and said the house where another woman would say I. She fed the fire and told it the thaw when a man from Greybank spoke of a counting room shut in the war; if she connected any of it to her own roof she put the connection in the private roll nobody is shown, but she did not connect it. On Ilmen 29 she laid one thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, and fetched no broom for either. On Silt 1 she stood over a new hairline of grey in the corner with a broom in her hand and did not sweep, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it goes; she touched the widow’s mark before the opening and at no other hour, not for the new grey, not for a basket, not at a bank.

\textbf{Ch 14.} Through Silt 2–8 she kept the house the way she kept the fire: instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and a half-pace kept from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the well. She told the fire it was the thaw when the brook came up clay-heavy behind the racks and again when the ice was called honeyed all through, and stood over the new grey in the corner without sweeping it, finer than the old clean dark line beside it. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark hung where it hung, untouched at a rack, a basket, a well, a door and a bed. On Silt 5 she carried him three doors down, set the basket inside the finger’s-width-open door away from any open slate, stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote, and asked nothing about the writing or the tin; the little-door burn shut on nothing. At dusk each day she set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft and put the fold right without looking at his face, carrying one crust and an empty place through seven days without a name.

\textbf{Ch 15.} Through Silt 9–15 she kept the house the way she kept the fire: every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace kept from every open slate at the Fishstairs, the Cross, the racks and three doors down in House Silt. She carried him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back, and when the water went around the clean dark line she stood over it and the new finer grey beside it with a broom in her hand and swept neither, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it went. A neighbour said the house had been saved and she did not. On Silt 14 she gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Round it / Go around}), went wide around the space under the lowest rack, and did not answer Jorra’s silence about the room off the shed. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark was not touched once, not at a rack, a shore, a step or a bed. It is told of her that she once sat up three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everybody was kind; she did not go toward the child in the yard whose foot stayed cold, and the boy did not lay the two together. At dusk of the last day she carried him up at the half-pace, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped. One brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold with the empty place beside it unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\textbf{Ch 16.} Through Days 75–77 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, and \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. The flood has gone out of the yard and left mud, and the sweeping goes around the clean dark line at the Vail corner, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack; she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody (\emph{Go around. It cost enough to come in. It’ll cost more to take out.}), stands over the two lines with a broom in her hand and sweeps neither, and tells the fire it is the thaw. The yard counts what the water took in loaves, glances and a space at the row’s end that nobody calls a number, and when a woman asks for a figure she tells her to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. She keeps the half-pace from every open slate, goes wide around a slate set out to dry at the well’s edge and does not touch the widow’s mark, because a well is not an opening and a basket is not a door. At the well she does not look at the quick child in cast-offs or at the warm loaf in his pocket and does not connect the man from Slate Row with either; if she saw the passing she put it where she puts the other things she does not enter, in the private roll nobody is shown. No opening came in three days and the mark hung where it hung. At dusk each day she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one brown-edged crust lies stiff in the fold with the empty place beside it unnamed and no third comes. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the mud, the half-beat, the loaf, the man from Slate Row, the two unswept lines and the empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
In Chapter 1 she is a hand in a doorway and a shadow, not a speaking part. Woodsmoke and wet wool arrive ahead of her; then the burn shaped like a little door reaches for the heat at the child’s belly, finds none, hovers over the bundle and withdraws. In Chapter 2 she is inside the house for the first time on the page and is known by its objects before she is known by her words: the hollow seat, the salt coat, the Ash ridge a thumb and then two thumbs wide, the charred edge of a slate nobody picks up, the roll the house keeps and does not show. She announces the taking, is answered by her son, refuses the answer by getting quieter, and on the third day performs the taking with a hand that knows how much a thing will bear. She lays the boy on a bed and tells the fire what to do. In Chapter 3 she takes that keeping out of the house for the first time and into a market that explains him as a figure. She carries him in a basket, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, refuses to say whose house he is beyond \emph{the house}, refuses to answer Berr about the mark, and walks him home without a word about where they have been. The private roll and the Court’s slate are seen to be the same shape of account, both entering a child who has not agreed to either, and her little-door hand is at one end of it. She has not explained any of it. Her silence has stopped being a pause and become a wall, and the wall has acquired a second face in the district’s grammar of entered kindness.

On Days 5 and 6 the keeping goes on without an entry. She touches the widow’s mark before the kiln on Stone 11 and at no other time, banks the coals with the back of a broken pot at dusk on Stone 12 and does not touch the mark then; she feeds the boy from her own dish and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She carries him to the Drawing and places the basket where he can see the work and cannot be part of it, never where a slate lies open, and stands a half-pace off with her little-door burn shut on nothing, refusing by her stillness to tell him what is being done. She says nothing about where they went, what was taken or from whom; when Jorra says \emph{the back room’s cold} she shifts the damper instead of answering. The wall has acquired a door she will not open and a room she will not enter, and the fire inside the rule of the mark goes on holding.

On Days 7, 8 and 9 the keeping goes on without an entry and adds no explanation. She opens the kiln under a hand that touches the mark and lets it go, feeds the foundling from the house’s dish and says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She carries him down twice through the cold off the Slip Brook and sets him in the bridge’s shade on a patch no slate has reached, the same care she used at the edge of the light at the Drawing; she stands a half-pace from every open slate and buys eels without counting them with her fingers. At the bank she does not touch the mark, and at the end of Stone 15 she goes around the days to Kindling in the arrangement of loaves and bits and comes back to the same place twice, so that the number need never be said. The wall has grown a second face: it keeps out the woman at the eels, the crust in the fold, the cuff on the bridge and the count her son will not speak, and it keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 10 through 14 the keeping goes on without an entry and the shape of the number becomes a household’s whole arithmetic. She touches the mark only before an opening --- not at a bank, not at the reading on Account-day --- and moves her lips along the loaves so the days to Kindling are a shape no collector can take up. She stands a half-pace from every open slate in the yard and at the Cross, refuses a neighbour a number with \emph{the house} and \emph{ask the pot}, and carries the basket down and back saying nothing about where they have been or what was read over him. On Stone 19 she moves the basket out of a draught without looking at his face and calls it nothing; she measures the Ash by thumb and leaves both ridges for the Last Day. The crust in the fold goes cold and stays where it was put. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour with the slate, the clerk’s soft sentence, the figure at the moot and the number her son will not speak, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 15 through 24 the keeping takes the measure of a tend and a year. The rule of the mark holds before each opening and at no bank or reading; the household’s number lives in loaves moved along a shelf, in the space at the end of the kindling and in a fist shut on a door-latch, and she will not say it even when the district gives out three and then two. She sends Tarn for a collector and carries the boy to the neighbour’s room, setting him where he can see and not join, with a half-pace kept from the open slate. At the Last Day’s sweeping she measures the ridge against the death-house’s with a thumb laid flat first, and lets the woman at the tubs say the grey will be left and burned and called dealt with. On Stone 30 she carries him down to the year’s last market for a reading and not an opening, stands a half-pace off with her burn shut, and brings him back under the roof to his bed, banked coals and two crusts in the fold she has neither named nor removed. The wall has acquired no door in ten days: it keeps out the neighbour with the fist, the clerk’s soft sentence, the figure read over the basket and the number Tarn will not speak, and keeps the boy warm without entering the warmth.

On Days 25 through 30 the keeping takes the measure of the Five and crosses the turn of the year. The year’s fire comes into the house in a clay dish from hands along the yard, and she touches the mark once before the opening and at no other hour --- a rule that holds as exactly on Ilmen 1, where there is no opening, as it held inside Y.H. 812. She says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gives every instruction to the fire and the wool, and enters neither the flame nor its payer. At the Weighing she keeps her half-pace from the slates and does not repeat the name the clean voice reads; at the Long Night she banks the fire and keeps the dark with stories; at the Remembering she goes around Garl’s name as around Ash left in a corner; on the Last Day she measures both ridges with one thumb and will not let the grey be swept early. On Ilmen 1 a neighbour calls the burned Ash dealt with, and she does not; the coals stay banked, the mark stays untouched, the two crusts stay in the fold, and she carries the keeping into 813 without explaining any of it. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the warmth, the name read at the Weighing, the reading in the next room and the year the district has already entered on its slates, and keeps the boy warm without entering the warmth.

On Days 31 through 37 the keeping takes the measure of the first warm days of the new year and adds no explanation. She says \emph{the house} and gives every instruction to the fire, the bucket and the wool; the half-pace from Alda and the turned slate stand in for the arrangement again; the widow’s mark is touched before the opening on Ilmen 6 and at no other hour, not at the bank, not for a date, not for a nearly full sound. She feeds him from the house’s own dish, puts the fold right without looking at his face, neither takes out nor names either crust, and carries him three doors down to the shade of the nineteen steps and back up the yard at dusk. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the warmth, the fourth note under a floorboard, the number in a fist at the well and the cough three doors down that everybody calls weather.

On Days 38 through 44 the keeping takes the measure of a death the Court does not enter and adds no explanation. She holds the basket on the bank with her feet apart in the wet clay while the yard lifts Dessa Silt out with their hands, and turns the boy’s face toward what is being done rather than away. She does not send for a collector and nobody remarks on it; the household goes to the fire and to its buckets instead, and warmth left where it fell and the morning came. On Ilmen 11 she measures the clean dark line where the Vail Ash turned its corner against the ridge two doors down, lays one thumb in each and carries the knowledge back without saying which was which; she does not fetch a broom. On Ilmen 13 she fetches a clay jar from House Silt, sets the basket just inside a door standing a finger’s width open, opens no slate and turns no errand into a visit to a bank, then sets the jar on the shelf by the wall at home. On Ilmen 14 and 15 she carries the boy upriver and leaves him in shade where no slate lies, stands a half-pace off a woman with a slate under her arm on the way home, and sets him on his bed at dusk with the fold put right and no look at his face. The private roll stays unshown, the wall acquires no door, and she has said nothing about the payer of any warmth or the woman in the water.

On Days 45 through 47 the keeping takes the measure of three days after the blessing and adds no explanation. She carries him under the north bridge and back at a half-pace from every open slate and sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without a look at his face. The mark is touched once before the opening on Day 45 and at no other hour --- not at a dusk bank, not for a date, not for a nearly full sound, not for the carrying of a basket. The month’s days go around in loaves moved along a shelf, a glance at the clay jar on the wall shelf and the space where a loaf should stand; at the well she goes around an open slate as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it over, and tells a neighbour the house sent the number up the road. She feeds him from the house’s own dish and does not say who paid for the milk. She does not touch the mark when the smoky crust goes out of the fold on Day 46, does not say that it is gone, and does not go around it with a broom. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the payer of the coal that went up with a bird, the hand that took the crust, the number that passed from fist to mouth to shoulder, and a woman dead nine mornings with no collector called.

On Days 48 through 54 the keeping takes the measure of seven more days of thaw and adds no explanation. She tells the fire it is the thaw, gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and says the house where another woman would say I; at the well and at the racks she goes at a half-pace from every open slate, goes around a slate propped at the rack end as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, and does not touch the widow’s mark, because a well is not an opening. On Account-day she sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carries him home saying nothing about what was read over him. Each dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft and puts the fold right without looking at his face. She stands a half-pace off while Alda writes and does not ask what was written, and says nothing about the payer of any warmth or about the woman dead sixteen mornings with no collector called. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the slack frame, the silence where an argument stood, the fifth note under a floorboard, the number that went from fist to mouth to shoulder, and the omission nobody will name.

On Days 55 through 60 the keeping takes the measure of the approach to Silt and the month named for what the river does, and adds no explanation. She tells the fire it is the thaw when a stranger at the well speaks of a sealed counting room and men dead of the breath, and she does not join the story to the kiln under her own roof; whatever she would put away she puts in the private roll nobody is shown, and there is nothing to put away. On Ilmen 27 she carries the basket three doors down into House Silt, sets it just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and away from any open slate, straightens a chipped cup and does nothing else; she stands a half-pace from Alda and the birth-slates and asks nothing. Her instruction goes to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and she says the house where another woman would say I. The stores go around in loaves and glances and a space at the row’s end that she does not call a number; the days to Silt are three, two, whatever the moot will say, and she gives the boy no figure. On Ilmen 29 she lays one thumb flat in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, a finger’s width wider, and fetches no broom for either, while the yard prepares a sweeping done a month ago. At the last market she keeps the half-pace, sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carries him home at dusk. On Silt 1 she stands over a fresh hairline of grey beside the clean dark line with a broom in her hand and does not sweep, saying it is the thaw; the mark is touched before the kiln is opened and not for the grey, a basket or a bank, and the carried fire keeps four, four and a gap under blind ash. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the Greybank story, the new grey, the withheld number, the sixth note that was not written and the woman dead twenty-two mornings with no collector called.

On Days 61 through 67 the keeping takes the measure of a week in which the river rises and the district calls it weather, and adds no explanation. She gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, three doors down in House Silt and at the well. She tells the fire it is the thaw when the brook comes up clay-heavy and when the ice is honeyed all through, and the new hairline of grey in the Vail corner lies finer than the old clean dark line and is not swept because the house says it is the thaw. There is no opening in any of the seven days, so the widow’s mark is not touched once, not at a rack, a well, a door or a basket. In House Silt she stands a half-pace off while Alda lays the slates writing-down and writes what she will not leave lying, and asks nothing; the arrangement between the two women holds without a word, a wall with a door neither opens. Each dusk she carries him up at a half-pace, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and puts the fold right without looking at his face. The private roll stays unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the higher water has given her nobody to answer. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the sixth page, the gone stone, the second cord, the clerk’s slate and the rising river, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 68 through 74 the keeping takes the measure of a flood that comes up around everything the house has left where it lies and then goes down again, and adds no explanation. She carries him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back at the half-pace, says \emph{the house}, gives every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, and tells the fire it is the thaw when a neighbour says the house was saved. The Ilm comes up over the Fishstairs, stands on the second step at the Cross on Account-day, and goes around both the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the burned line two doors down; she stands over the standing line and the new finer grey with a broom and sweeps neither, and gives the broom its instruction before anybody. No opening comes in seven days and the widow’s mark is not touched once. On Silt 13 she carries him three doors down and back with the door a finger’s width open and no slate opened, and asks nothing about the sixth page or the tin; the arrangement with Alda holds without a word. She does not go down to the child in the yard whose foot stays cold, though it is told of her that she once sat three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everyone was kind, and the boy does not lay the two together. At dusk of the last day she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, and leaves the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the flood, the cold foot, the two lines and the empty place beside the one crust, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 75 through 77 the keeping takes the measure of a recovery that is another kind of avoidance. The yard sweeps around what the water left and calls the new grey thaw, and she stands over both lines with a broom and sweeps neither; a figure goes from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrives nowhere, and she answers a woman who wants it by sending her to the pot. A warm loaf passes from a man from Slate Row into a foundling’s pocket with no slate between them, and she neither looks nor connects the two. The half-pace, the unentered basket, the untouched mark and the private roll all hold exactly as they held before the flood; the wall has acquired no door, and the boy is still not written as Vail.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Did not enter the birth room and said nothing. Woodsmoke and wet wool came ahead of her, then the cold off the yard, then the hand with the little-door burn across its back --- lintel, threshold, two straight sides. It felt for heat at the child’s belly, found none, opened and shut once above the covered bundle and withdrew. She stepped back out into the Clay Yard without looking at child or women. The crust and the warmed stone had already come from her hearth, neither entered against anybody; the kiln breathed through the wall afterward. She still intends to take him on the third day.

\item Ch 2: Kept the fire and the house through Days 2 and 3. At first light touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln and at no other time, gave instruction to the pot and the fire, would not let anyone fill Garl’s seat or take his coat down, and said the house kept a roll of its own. Announced that the boy would come under the roof and was answered \emph{he’s not Vail}; got quieter and did not reply. On the third morning came for him, crossed to the bench first, lifted him with the little-door hand, said \emph{the boy} and \emph{the house}, carried him up the Clay Yard and laid him on fresh straw. Gave the bed to the foundling and the loft to Tarn without explaining either, told the pot it would pay for itself in the thaw, and left the charred slate in the kiln ash untouched.

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. Carried the boy out of the kiln-house in a basket under a fold of wool --- he left the house and its heat went out behind him --- and held him like a pot filled that must not be slopped. Did not touch the widow’s mark, since the coals were only being banked. Counted off the question of the mother with \emph{Account-day} and the question of the house with \emph{the house}; put the fold back over his face and ears without looking and spoke the instruction to the wool and the wind. Kept a half-pace from the slate on the block and did not set the basket where it lay open. At the Slate Row end refused to answer Berr about the confirmed widow’s mark, pulled the wool over the boy’s ear, and let the uncalled debt lie. Lifted the basket off the post in the late afternoon and turned back up the Clay Yard without a word about where they had been or what had been read over the top of him; the wool smelled of woodsmoke and the door did not quite shut.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. On Stone 11 touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln and at no other time, fed the household from her own dish, put the fold right without looking and gave the instruction about the draught to the fire.
