A tile debt left lying — No term entered — Grey, unmeasured — Nowhere; not forgiven\par

Bread given at a house door — No entry — Nothing — Nothing; given and not entered\par

A loan that can hear — The term of the debt — What the borrower hears — By the lender, who does not always call\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The woman who came on the last Account-day had six years in her thumb and wanted me to write seven. I wrote the day of entering, which her household had set, and not the six she carried. She said the seventh was as good as kept. I said a kept year and a paid year are different vessels, which is a thing I have no right to say at a counter, and so I said nothing and let her say it. The ordinance gives me no word for the year a man holds back so that he need not pay. I have scored a line in the lower margin with my knife instead, which is not an entry and cannot be added.\end{quote}

\subsection*{III. Of the keeping of those in service}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A bond-servant is lodged apart from the household’s children, in the loft or the out-room, and is not entered at the family hearth. The household’s own child is not lodged there.

\item Where consent to a lawful collection is withheld, the vessel is clip-held by the wrist until consent is entered. A pale ring left at the wrist is spoken of as nothing and is not entered as a wound.

\item No cold iron is set to a living wrist save by the officer appointed thereunto. The tubes are mended at the smithy, which keeps no kiln-mark and is not a great house.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} A foundling was given a bed under the roof here, in a house three doors down the yard, while a debt was given the loft. The house did not call it kindness and I have not entered it. A child under a roof and a debt above a wheel-shed are two vessels in one house, and the house knows which it means to keep. I have put no figure against either.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} The ring shows through the winter. I have seen a man rub his cuff down over it while he was being told the figure, and go out saying the ring would go in the thaw. That is what my mother said about everything. It is not in the ordinance.\end{quote}

\subsection*{IV. Of assignment and purchase before due}

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item A debt may be assigned before it is due, and the assignment entered in the hand of the buyer or his factor. The debtor is not asked.

\item Where a debt is bought for the measure rather than the marks, the entry is made in marks. The measure is not entered.

\item The widow’s mark is not assigned. The factor at Greybank confirms it, and the confirmation is spoken of as a kindness and entered as one.

\item Debts of Grath sold south to the bowls of Sere are entered as goods and not as persons. The figure is copied from the factor’s slate.

\end{enumerate}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the leaning hand of the factor’s man come up from Greybank, written over article 11:} assigned in due course. \emph{Underneath, in mine:} bought before due. He strikes the verb wherever he finds one, as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff and sell at the crossing. I have left both stand. A debt bought before it is due has a different smell in the room from one assigned in due course, and I am the man who has to stand at the counter when the smell arrives.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Margin:} Against article 13 the factor’s man wrote \emph{kindness entered}, which is exactly what the ordinance says and exactly what the house means when it does not want a question. There is no column for it and no figure in it, and still it is entered every time.\end{quote}

\subsection*{V. Of faults and their correcting}

Fault — As entered — Correction\par

A verb in the roll — Page copied again, in the same hand — The verb set underneath, where the clerk put it\par

A debt in a house roll only — Stands — Not paid, and not called forgiven\par

A term called \emph{till the thaw} — The day of entering — If no day stands, none is supplied\par

A seventh year claimed early — Six, and the seventh held — No figure given to the holding\par

A sealed bond carried beyond the room — The carrier’s own debt entered in its place — The first entry left standing beside it\par

\subsection*{The form of entry}

\emph{Set out at the end of Title the Fourth. I have copied it with the blanks as they stand in the book. In nine years nobody has filled one.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Entered this day, being ---day of -------, in the year of the Hearth ------, the debt of ----------------------, set at -------- marks, or ------- loaves, or ------- days of service, to be served from the day of entering and not from the thaw; the interest to gather as grey in the house account; the hand that writes not the hand that holds; the debt to stand until claimed, and to be discharged where the household says. Entered by ----------------------, who is not the man who heard it.\end{quote}

\subsection*{Seven lines pasted inside the cover}

\emph{Not part of the ordinance. Said under the breath at the counter while the tally is cut, and never when the factor’s man is in the room. I found the leaf pasted in and have not taken it out.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Six on the sill and a seventh not cut,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wood keeps the year that the slate left out;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape grey in the corner and crust by the door,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape what nobody claimed stands and stands, and no more.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the house says the thaw, and the thaw says a sum;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the notch is a place and the slate is a figure,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place goes on when the figure is done.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand, against the last line:} Seven lines pasted. \emph{In mine:} I count seven and so does he. He has put no number against the notch, which is how I know he has looked at it. A man does not number what he has not looked at.\end{quote}

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The brown at the head is iron-gall and mine, made by holding the quire open through a market morning; it will not come out of the creases. The bone-pale streak in the gutter is slip off the forearms of a thrower who held her slate away from her coat while she waited and set it for a moment against this leaf. The line scored deep in the lower margin is mine and was cut with the small knife I keep at the counter, the same morning the woman wanted six called seven; a knife goes into paper more easily than into a bench, but the mark stays in both. The tallow at the fold came off the lamp I keep turned low while I write, so that a woman at the counter will not change her tale for me. The grey along the outer edge came off my own cuff going down to the Cross on Account-day, where I put my hand into a corner I had no business putting it into. The green bead in the corner is not slip; it is lead glaze from a girl come up from High Kiln with the sweetness still at her mouth, who leaned to see the form of entry and did not ask to have it filled. I have kept everything where it fell. There is no Last Day behind a counter.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody has claimed}

\begin{quote}\itshape Under the roof they count in loaves; above the wheel they count in years; and the bench counts both in wood and says neither thing.\end{quote}

I have asked the factor’s man, a man come down from the College, and a woman who stood here about her house, and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before. I have left the line where it was written. Tomorrow the factor’s man will come up from Greybank with a debt bought before it is due and want the entry in his own hand, and I shall write \emph{bought} underneath as I have written it every tend; a woman will come with six years in her thumb and ask me to make them seven, and I shall write the day that stands. The bench behind the counter has six notches cut into it and a seventh place scored deep with a knife and not cut through. I did not cut it and cannot say who did. It will be there in the morning.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Book of Worth, Being the Valuations Set in the Assessor’s House at Sill in the Thin Year, and the Figures Set Above Them in a Second Hand}
\CRsheetheading{The Book of Worth, Being the Valuations Set in the Assessor’s House at Sill in the Thin Year, and the Figures Set Above Them in a Second Hand}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the valuation ledger of the assessor’s house in Slate Row, Sill; figures in Ledgerhand, terse remarks in the hand of the assessor who set them, one column left unfilled, and two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the College · Written at Sill in the assessor’s house built in Y.H. 776, in the Thin Year Y.H. 812, and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813; kept in a board cover under the counter and taken down when a figure is disputed. It survives as two leaves of foolscap sewn with wire: an iron-gall thumb at the head, a streak of bone-pale slip down the gutter, a green bead of glaze in the lower corner, a tallow thumb, grey Ash worked into the outer fold, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the College’s narrow hand, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I set the worth of vessels in this house. It stands in Slate Row at Sill, built in Y.H. 776, with the Court’s room next door and the Waiting Room behind, and the slate on my counter was bought the year the house was raised and has outlasted three assessors whose names I cannot now read. A figure comes to me off the collector’s slate and I set a worth against it and a return due; once a tend a man comes down from the College at the Hearthseat and strikes the verbs out of what I have written. I put them back. It is an arrangement of the kind that lasts because neither of us writes in the other’s hand.

The brown thumb at the head of this leaf is iron-gall and mine, made by holding a quire open through a market morning. It will not wash out of the creases. There are clerks in the Hearthseat who can tell an assessor by his thumb before he has spoken a word, which is one of the small mercies of the trade.

What follows is one leaf of the valuation book, being the figures set in the last tend of Stone and carried forward into Ilmen. I have set the rates first, so that a man may see what an ember is said to be worth before he sees what I set against a life. I have not added the column. Adding is a College matter, and the last time a hand in this house added a column the total would not agree with the printed one, and the factor at Greybank sent word that the printed one was to be copied again in a better hand.

\subsection*{The rates of the house}

Entry — As the house has it\par

Copper bit — twelve to a silver mark\par

Silver mark — twenty to a gold crown, a Sere coin that does not stay in Grath\par

Ember — five marks, by the Court’s book; no man has exchanged one for the other\par

Newborn vessel — twelve to fifteen embers\par

Labourer in good case — forty to sixty embers\par

A Held vessel — a hundred and upward\par

One of the Kept — three hundred; no figure any household can spend\par

Deduction — one in twelve, as the notice says\par

Whole return — one measure poured into one vessel, booked at the figure\par

Thin return — many measures pooled and divided, figure entered by lot\par

An ember is worth five marks in this room. In the yard a woman sells six eels for five marks or five for six and makes nothing of it, which is a fact about eels and not about embers. I have set both figures down and joined neither.

\subsection*{The leaf, as it stood}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand. The remarks are mine, in the hand that set the worth, and are not part of the account.}

Vessel, as entered — Embers — Worth — Deduction — Return due — Remark\par

A thrower of the low yard, second entry — 41 — 205 marks — 1 in 12 — thin — First entry stood higher. No reason entered.\par

A glaze-room girl, High Kiln — 38 — 190 marks — 1 in 12 — thin — Sweetness at the mouth. Name given, not entered.\par

A widow with the mark, Vail house — 33 — not set — 1 in 12 — — — The mark is not a figure. House roll kept close. Kindness entered.\par

A clay-bound hand, the terraces — 44 — 220 marks — 1 in 12 — thin — Six years entered. The seventh held back.\par

A man of the Weir — 47 — 235 marks — 1 in 12 — thin — Drawn before light. Worth set after. Order as it stood.\par

A foundling left at the mill — 12 — 60 marks — 1 in 12 — — — A stone under him, not a name. Stands till a hearth claims him.\par

Forty of Low Kiln, one line for the batch — — — — — 1 in 12 — whole — By lot. Names not taken. Purchaser entered elsewhere.\par

One of the Kept, in passing — 300 — not set — none — none — Asked after the weather. Pity entered.\par

A vessel returned three times — 29 — 145 marks — 1 in 12 — whole — Figure smaller than the last. Entered whole. No note made.\par

A house of the terraces, disputed — 52 — 260 marks — 1 in 12 — — — Thumb wiped twice. Figure asked for, then not wanted. Left standing.\par

\subsection*{The remarks}

A remark is not part of the account. The College has never thought to strike the remark column out of this book, which I take for an oversight and not a mercy, and so I keep what I please in it. \emph{Figure smaller than the last} is the only line on this leaf that I have had to write twice. The first time I set it down as a cause and then scraped the word away, which is the bare square in the lower margin; the second time I set it down as a likeness, which is all it is. I have seen three entries of one vessel and three figures going the same way, smaller each time, and the deduction standing at one in twelve between them like a stone that has not moved while the water went down. I do not say what it means. A clerk who explains a figure has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\emph{Asked after the weather. Pity entered.} There is no column for pity and no figure for a courteous vessel. I put it in the remark because a man who has sat across this counter for nine and thirty years should be allowed one line that is not a number. The College left it. I have not decided whether that was the oversight.

\subsection*{What the College hand did}

The man from the Hearthseat has a cuff gone soft from washing and ink settled in two fingers of it. He does not sit down. He borrowed the leaf on a market morning and did three things to it.

Where I wrote \emph{the first entry stood higher}, he struck out \emph{stood} and set \emph{was higher} above, and then struck out \emph{was} also, leaving \emph{higher} with nothing to stand on. I have put \emph{stood} back underneath and left his \emph{higher} where he set it. A figure with a verb in it can be argued with, which is why he takes the verbs out; but a woman at my counter wants to know who did what, and a word with nothing to stand on will not tell her.

Against the vessel returned three times I had written, in the remark, \emph{with memory}. He struck it and set \emph{whole} above it. Both stand. \emph{Whole} is the word the notice uses and the word the household hears read in a clean voice at the Weighing. \emph{With memory} is the word I use when I am not reading anything aloud. I have not chosen between them, and I would thank any man who told me I had to.

He struck my last column also and wrote \emph{No such column} above it. I have struck his striking out and left the column where I drew it.

\subsection*{The column I drew and they struck out}

I keep a place beside the figure the notice gives for the figure the household actually gave. I have set no heading over it. A heading would make it an account, and an account is a thing a man may be called to answer for, and this house has answered for enough this year.

The last time I was asked to set a worth against a house of Low Kiln, the man who came did not bring the figure in his mouth. He brought it in his thumb, the way they do down the yard, and wiped that thumb twice across his slate before he touched nothing and said the figure the notice says. I entered the figure the notice says, as I am required to, and in the place beside it I entered his two wipes and the pause between them, which is not a figure and cannot be added. When the College man struck the column he wrote \emph{No such column} in the same upright hand he uses for the deduction. He had counted the rows before he wrote it, which is how I know the column troubled him. A man does not count what he has not looked at.

A place is not a debt. The College teaches eleven words for a deduction and has none for a place, and the clerk who came down from the Hearthseat gave himself away by putting a number in one.

\subsection*{In the margins}

The streak of slip in the gutter came off the forearms of the thrower whose figure stands second on the leaf. She held her slate away from her coat while she waited and set it against this quire for a moment, and the grey came off on the edge. The green bead in the lower corner is not slip. It is lead glaze from a girl who leaned over to see the writing with the sweetness still at her mouth, and touched the paper, and said nothing. I left it where she put it. The tallow thumb at the foot of the second leaf is the foundling’s, or the mark of a woman holding him who used her whole hand to keep the leaf still in the draught under the door; I do not know which and have not asked. The Ash in the outer fold came off my own cuff going down to the Cross on Account-day, where I put my hand into a corner I had no business putting it into and the grey came away on the cloth. They sweep the corners of the houses on the Last Day and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a valuation book.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The line below was not written by me and is not in Ledgerhand. I found it under the counter when I came in on the morning after the last market, and I asked the factor’s man, and the College man, and a woman who had stood at the counter about her house, and had three answers and no hand. I have left it where it was written.

\begin{quote}\itshape The book keeps the figure. The yard keeps the place where the figure stood.\end{quote}

The leaf goes back under the counter. Tomorrow the factor’s man will come up from Greybank with a slate whose upper line is in a neat dark hand, with a small stop between two clusters that I have seen before and joined to nothing, and I shall set a worth against it and put the verbs back and leave the column where I drew it. A woman will stand where women stand and ask what her house is worth, and I shall read her the figure the notice says, which is the only figure she can carry away. The other one stays here. It has nowhere else to go.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Clicking in the Reed, Being a Hunter’s Notes on the Reed-Wolf of the East Marsh}
\CRsheetheading{The Clicking in the Reed, Being a Hunter’s Notes on the Reed-Wolf of the East Marsh}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A reed-cutter’s field book on one beast, set down as a record of hunts and not a book of natural philosophy; the calls and the counting-song in Grathic, the tally in charcoal and reed-sap, with a Stonemouth tooth-buyer’s corrections in Ledgerhand in the margin · Written in the hunting month of Bone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by a reed-cutter of Reedholt who went into the east marsh with a spear and a knot of cord, and who hunts still; copied forward in Bone, Y.H. 813. Set on the backs of Stonemouth weigh-slips gone soft with damp and on two folded sheets of birch bark, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a bark wrap under a loose board of the hunter’s hut. It survives stained and used: a tooth-grey smear along the fore-edge where the book was wiped on a sleeve after a kill, a press of wet reed across the first leaf, a brown peat thumb at the tally, a small round mark where a buyer set a two-mark piece down and left it, and a line of figures in the narrow hand of the Stonemouth weigh-clerk who counted and paid for the teeth. The hunter has answered that clerk in the foot and has not struck a word of his out.\par}\medskip
I cut reed at the east marsh and I have kept this book three winters. It is not a book of natural philosophy. I have no slate-name and no learning, and I set down only what I have put my hand to. A man who writes what he has heard from a hearth is writing a hearth, not a beast. I have known both kinds of book and this is the second sort, being the sort a man can use.

The brown thumb at the tally is peat, not Ash. There is Ash enough on the beast without bringing it into the book. I have not washed any of it off. A book that has never been wiped on a sleeve was never taken into the marsh.

\subsection*{The voice of it}

It does not howl. This is the first thing a new man gets wrong and the thing that gets him bitten. A wolf that howls is a wolf you can walk away from; you know where it stands and it knows you know. The mouth in the reed makes a low clicking with the tongue, under the water’s noise, so that you hear it in your boots before you hear it in the air. It carries over water as a man’s talk carries over a floor. Four clicks, then a gap, then four again, and the gap is where it is listening.

I have set the call down below as we use it, answered across the water to draw them to a stand. It is not a song for a fire. It is a thing said under the breath with the tongue behind the teeth, and the words are only there to keep the count for the men who cannot click true.

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the mud and one for the slack,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes to the warm and it comes to the crack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it comes not for singing, it comes for the place\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where the way runs shallow and under the face.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Click once in the reed, then hold, then click:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a man who runs is a man they pick.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Stand to the elbow. Show them the bare.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It wants the one place and it finds it there.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five in the open and nine in the wet,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one goes still and the rest go yet;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and leave the fourth for the man who lacked.\end{quote}

A reed-cutter goes in pairs. This is not a kindness. If a man goes alone into the east marsh in Bone he will come back with one arm or he will not come back, and the pairs are because a beast that has opened a way in one man must be driven off the other before it finishes. The last line of the song is for the one who does not come back. We leave the fourth click for him and we do not say his name at it. There is a man at Reedholt with two fingers gone who clicks four for himself and a fifth he will not explain, and I have let him keep it.

\subsection*{How it kills}

It goes for the throat and the inside of the elbow. That is the whole of it; there is no wrestling and no throwing down. I have seen a Held man, a man who carried more than his natural measure and was twice the weight of me, go into the mud under one of these and be under before he could shape a shout. The mud did as much as the beast. A pack can pull down a Held man in mud, which is why we cut reed in pairs and why I have no fine opinion of my own standing among them.

It does not worry a victim. This is what the hearths get wrong when they say it worries. It opens one place and waits at it. I have watched from a stand with my spear across my knee and seen a beast open a man’s elbow and then lie with its jaw against the place and wait, as steady as a collector with a tube against a wrist. The man stopped struggling. The beast did not shake him or worry him or drag him. It kept the one place, and the warm went out of it, and when I drove it off the man was already a thing I would not have sent for a physician to save.

I will set down what I have seen and not what it means. It killed quickly, at one place, and there was no anger in it that I could see. A collector’s draw is the same work done with iron and a slate. I have stood near enough to a draw to know the smell of the cold iron and I have stood near enough to one of these to smell the wet wool and the mud, and the two smells are not the same, but the work is. I have thought about that more than is good for a reed-cutter and I have not written a cause.

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the hunts I kept a true account of. Some nights I did not write because my hands were full and some I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The figure in the fifth column is the Stonemouth figure, not mine. I counted teeth; the clerk counted marks.

Night — Place — Heard — Taken — Teeth — Marks — Lost\par

Bone 4 — East bank below Reedholt — five — two — six — 12 — a dog, bitten in the elbow, shot at dusk\par

Bone 9 — The marsh road cut — seven — three — nine — 18 — none\par

Bone 14 — Standing water north of Mud End — nine — two — five — 10 — one of ours, hand taken, lived\par

Bone 20 — The lower Ilm, silt side — five — one — three — 6 — none; the wind turned and we were heard\par

Bone 27 — Old run east of the reedbeds — seven — four — eleven — 22 — spear lost in the mud, not recovered\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{The narrow hand wrote against the “Heard” column:} five, seven, nine are not a number. Enter as 7. Average 7 to a pack, 6 teeth to a hunt. This is the figure the factor will ask for.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{And along the foot of the “Marks” column, in the same hand:} 12+18+10+6+22 = 68. Received. Account stands.\end{quote}

I had the book out at Stonemouth on Bone 30 and the weigh-clerk laid his cuff on the leaf before he looked at me, the way they do, and set the figures down. He is a clerk and I am a reed-cutter and the account is his, so I have left his hand standing. But a pack is five or seven or nine according to the night and there is no factor in the marsh to give it a number. He has put seven where I put three figures, and under it he has written \emph{average}, which is a word that means nothing to a man standing in water up to his calf with nine of them clicking in the dark.

\subsection*{The teeth and the pelt}

The teeth are set into clamp-handles, and a good tooth is worth two marks at Stonemouth. This is not a pretty trade and I have never pretended it is one. A tooth remembers the shape of a way; that is what the clamp-men say when they buy, and they pay for the saying. I have seen a handle set with one of these teeth bite true where an iron one would slip, and I have no explanation for it and no wish to make one. I took eleven teeth on Bone 27 and I would take the same again if it bought the winter.

The pelt is worth nothing. The hair carries Ash, and a coat of it makes a man go thin by degrees without his knowing how. I have seen a Fen trader try to sell one in Mud End with the Ash worked out of it, and he could not, because you cannot work Ash out of a thing, you can only move it somewhere else. We burn the pelts. We do not sell them and we do not keep them and we say so plainly when a man asks, because a man who buys a reed-wolf pelt is a man who will come back for another.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

The hearths say it is a drowned man’s grudge that has Learnt to click. There are songs about it in the Fenmarch with a man’s name in them and a wrong done at a weir. I have heard them and I have no quarrel with a song. But I have taken six-and-thirty of these in three winters and opened most of them, and what I found was a wolf. It is a wolf that took to the water and stayed there, and the cold of the water has gone into it the way the wet goes into a coat. It kills the way water kills, at one place and without wanting anything from the man it kills. I have written \emph{no anger} in the margin and the clerk has written over it:

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the clerk’s hand:} Malice: not entered. Sentiment is not a figure and has no place in a tally.\end{quote}

I did not write that it had no malice because I forgave it. I wrote it because I watched. Those are different things and a clerk’s hand cannot tell them apart, which is the whole reason I keep this book in a bark wrap under a board instead of on a slate in Stonemouth.

Two winters ago a man of Reedholt went in alone and came back walking in the direction he had been facing, and his mother lived in the next hut and did not know him. We did not send for a collector because there was nothing in him to draw, and because the collectors do not come into the east marsh in Bone. He walked to the water and stood, and in the morning he was not there. I have set this down because it happened and not because it explains anything. The hearths will make a song of it and put a name in it and the name will be wrong.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The tooth-grey along the fore-edge is from Bone 27, when I wiped my hand on the leaf before I could find a rag. The round mark is a two-mark piece the buyer set down and forgot; I have left it where it fell. The wet reed across the first leaf is from the morning the wind turned on us and we lay flat in the cut until the clicking went away. The peat thumb is mine. The clerk’s figures I have not touched, and the hunter’s hand that wrote \emph{no anger} under them is my own and will not be struck.

There is a new run east of the reeds that I have not walked. The water stands in it when it should have drained and the clicks come from it in fours with a longer gap than I have heard before. I do not know what the longer gap means. I will go in at the next Bone with a pair of cord and a fresh spear, and I will count them going and count them back, and if there are nine where there should be five I will set that down too, in my own hand, with the verb left in it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Collector’s Day-Book, Being the Measures Drawn in Sill and the Clay Towns from the Last Market of Stone in Y.H. 812 through the Five to the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813, with the Embers, the Deduction, and the Note the Vessel Gave}
\CRsheetheading{The Collector’s Day-Book, Being the Measures Drawn in Sill and the Clay Towns from the Last Market of Stone in Y.H. 812 through the Five to the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813, with the Embers, the Deduction, and the Note the Vessel Gave}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from an officer’s own pocket day-book; figures in Ledgerhand copied from the slate, the remarks in the hand that held the cold iron tube, a column of notes struck out by the College and drawn back by the officer, one figure struck and set above in a borrowed hand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written on the road between Sill and Greybank in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, through the Five and into Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates; carried in an oiled-paper wrap in the officer’s coat, beside the tube in its wool sleeve. It survives with grey at the head of the ember column, iron filings worked into the gutter from the tube’s wrap, a tallow thumb at the foot, a streak of bone-pale slip, a green bead of lead glaze in the lower corner, a damp tide-line from the Waiting Room, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of a clerk of the College, and one line at the foot nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I draw the measure. The clerk at Greybank sets the figure down; I hold the tube. There is a difference between the two, and it is not the difference the College would have you believe, which is the difference between a taking and a draw. A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way. The slate is the difference, and the slate is a piece of stone with a neat hand on it.

This book goes in my coat under oiled paper, and the tube goes beside it in a sleeve of wool. When I hold the leaf still in the draught under a door my fingers leave grey on it. I have washed them. The grey is the trade, and the trade is the only kin I have: no house, no name but the slate-name upon the roll, and a cuff that has gone soft from washing. I do not set that name on this leaf. A name written in a book that may be read by a woman whose house I have entered is a name that can be called back to her door, and I have called at enough doors.

What follows is one leaf, from the last market of Stone through the Five and into the first tend of Ilmen. Twelve copper bits to a silver mark; twenty marks to a gold crown, a Sere coin that does not stay in Grath. An ember is booked at five marks and no man has exchanged one for the other. A newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen, a labourer in good case forty to sixty, and one of the Kept three hundred, which is a figure no household can spend. One in twelve is printed on the notice and read twice at the Cross. I have put no second figure beside it in the ember column. I have put it in the column beside that one, which the College struck out.

Draws on this leaf: nine. Lines with no draw in them: two. Figures struck: one. Columns struck: one.

\subsection*{The leaf, as I set it down}

\emph{Figures in Ledgerhand, copied from the slate. The remarks are mine, in the hand that held the tube. The last column is mine also and is not part of the account.}

Day — Vessel, as the slate has it — Embers — Deduction — Banked to — Note — Remark\par

Stone 30 — A widow of the lower town. \emph{Loaf} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — Four loaves baked, three to the levy. Figure read twice, once for those that came late.\par

Stone 30 — Forty of Low Kiln. One slate for the batch, by lot — — — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — — — Held overnight in the Waiting Room. Birth-names not taken. A barrow of grey went out through the north gate in the afternoon.\par

Kindling — A man of Mud End. \emph{Peat} — 47 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — flat — Year’s first measure, taken before light. Kiln’s breath. The neighbours called it merciful.\par

Kindling — A child three days returned, Low Kiln. \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — none — Worse before dusk. Entered as a birth, not a worsening.\par

Weighing — A glaze-room girl, High Kiln. \emph{Sweet} — 38 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — nearly full — Pale line at the gum. Asked after her girl; not entered.\par

the Long Night — A clay-bound hand of the terraces. \emph{Seven} — 44 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — Consent withheld. Clip-held by the wrist until consent entered. Draw made by lamp; no fire after dusk.\par

the Remembering — One of the Kept, in passing. No slate-name — 300 — none — none — none — Asked after the weather. Pity entered, which has no column.\par

the Last Day — A house of the terraces, disputed. \emph{Shoulder} — 52 — 1 in 12 — — — flat — Thumb wiped twice before touching nothing. Figure asked for, then not wanted. Left standing.\par

Ilmen 1 — A thrower of the low yard. \emph{Nineteen} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — First entry of the new roll. Earlier figure struck; no reason entered.\par

Ilmen 10 — A man of the Weir. \emph{Eel} — 52 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — full — Drawn before light. Pale round place left on the arm. The bell went four, four and a gap; nobody crossed.\par

Ilmen 10 — No vessel drawn. A clerk set at the Fishstairs — — — — — — — — — Cuff grey from washing; slate held to the forearm; hand to slate before eyes to the stalls. I asked whose measure it was. Nobody had called one. Not one of ours.\par

\subsection*{The note column}

Before the tube I set a knuckle on the wall or the rim of the cup. A whole vessel answers full. One cracked through answers flat, a small dead sound that stops at the surface. A vessel with air under the note answers nearly full, and the yards have no word for it, so I have set down the phrase as I heard it, which is not Grathic and will not be read at a Weighing. A vessel turned toward in expectation may give nothing at all; I have entered that as \emph{none} and not as a nought, because a nought is a figure and a silence is not.

The kiln-masters of Sill know the full note and keep it to themselves, which is their right and their trade. I know it because I have stood in forty rooms where a pot was set down and the whole house went on talking over the sound of it. A collector who cannot hear a vessel is a man who draws blind. He will still bring back his figure. The figure will still be entered. That is the trouble with figures.

On Weighing I wrote \emph{nearly full} for the girl of the glaze room, and the clerk borrowed the leaf and struck the whole column out. He wrote \emph{No such column} above it in his narrow upright hand. I have drawn the column back underneath and left his words standing over it. He had to look at every row before he could write that there were none worth entering, and I watched him do it. A note is not a figure and cannot be added, which is why he struck it, and a figure cannot hear a vessel, which is why I put it back.

\subsection*{The grey}

The grey at the head of the ember column came off my own fingers while I gave the figure to the clerk at Greybank on a market morning. It is the colour of skimmed milk gone off. It goes in under the nails first and comes up into the creases by the second year, and after that a man may wash until the water freezes and nothing changes. The filings in the gutter came out of the wool sleeve the tube rides in; there is always a little iron in the fold, and it has never once drawn the warmth out of the paper, which is a mercy of a kind and the only one in this book.

The tallow thumb at the foot is mine, from holding the lamp low while I wrote in a room where somebody was saying something I wanted the end of. The streak of slip came off a thrower’s forearms when she set her slate beside mine to wait for a figure. The green bead is lead glaze and not slip; a girl leaned over to see the writing with the sweetness still at her mouth, touched the leaf, said nothing, and went back to her terrace. I have not washed it off. The tide-line along the foot came from the Waiting Room, where the collected are kept overnight before banking and the damp gets into everything left on a bench. The bare square in the lower margin is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. I have not written the word back, and I have not forgotten it.

On the Last Day they sweep the corners of houses and burn what they find in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a coat.

\subsection*{What the two borrowed hands did}

The clerk from the College struck the figure of thirteen against the child on Kindling and set twelve above it, saying a vessel three days returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw. Both stand. I have asked which is right and neither of them has told me, and I have stopped asking, because an officer who asks after a correction is an officer who will soon be making one.

He struck a verb also. Where I wrote \emph{I drew} he set \emph{the measure was drawn} above, and underneath that he set \emph{the warmth was entered}, which is further from the bed than the first. I have put \emph{I drew} back beneath both. A sentence with nobody in it is a sentence no woman can ask about, and women ask about these draws in the end, always at the door, always after the tube is put away.

The other hand is not the College’s. It is a tall leaning hand from Greybank, and against \emph{the neighbours called it merciful} it wrote \emph{the draw was lawful} and underlined the word twice. Both stand. Lawful is true and does not mention a man on a bed in Mud End who was already gone when I came through the door. Merciful is what the neighbours said, and I set it down because it was said in my hearing and there is no column for what a room says after the tube comes out.

\subsection*{The verse the collectors carry up the yard}

\emph{Called under the breath going up the Clay Yard, never while the tube is out, and never twice in one house.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Cold iron, warm arm,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a hiss and a pale round ring;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the figure goes up and the figure goes down\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the note stays where it came in.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four and four and a place where the fifth should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape I carry the tube and the book in my coat\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the grey goes home ahead of me.\end{quote}

The man who sang this to me would not sing the last line while the factor’s man stood on the quay, which is how I know the last line is the one that matters. I have copied it as it came and put no gloss on it. A collector who explains a song has begun to write a sermon, and sermons get copied.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The figure is read twice. The note is read by nobody. Both were taken from the same vessel on the same morning.\end{quote}

I asked the clerk at Greybank, and a woman who stood at my counter about her house, and a man come down from Slate Row with a cuff gone soft, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written.

The book goes back into the oiled paper and the tube into its wool sleeve. Tomorrow the bell will go four, four and a gap with nobody crossing, and a figure will be read twice at the Cross, and I shall set the tube to a way and set the knuckle to the wall first, and write the note down before the College can strike it out. The grey will come off on the next leaf. I have stopped washing it.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Drawing Book, Being the Measures of the Sill District Entered at Greybank in the Last Tends of Stone, Y.H. 812}
\CRsheetheading{The Drawing Book, Being the Measures of the Sill District Entered at Greybank in the Last Tends of Stone, Y.H. 812}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A page from the tally-book of the Court’s collector’s clerk at Greybank; figures in Ledgerhand, with the officer’s remarks in the hand that made the draw · Written in the factor’s house at Greybank in Y.H. 812, the year the clay towns call the Thin Year, by the clerk who keeps the tally for Sill and the villages about; the officers are entered on the leaf and the clerk is not. Copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Y.H. 813. It survives as a quire of paper soft at the fore-edge in a tin on the factor’s shelf: a grey thumb at the head of the ember column, a streak of slip down the gutter, a green bead of glaze in the lower corner, a drag of Ash along the foot, one figure struck through and set above in a second hand, and a line at the foot which the factor’s clerk did not write.\par}\medskip
I keep the tally for the Sill district in the factor’s house at Greybank. The officer makes the draw and gives me the figure; I set it down. The figures go in Ledgerhand, without verbs, because a figure with a verb in it can be argued with and one without cannot. The remarks are the officer’s own, in the hand that held the tube, and I have not changed a word of them. The College would take the verbs out of those as well if it knew they were there. The factor allows them. He says a remark is not part of the account, which is his way of saying that a thing may be written down so long as it is never entered.

The grey at the head of the ember column came off on the officer’s fingers. He laid them on the page while he gave me the number and did not know he had marked it. I have not rubbed it out. It is the only mark on the leaf that I did not set here of purpose, and it is the one the factor’s clerk asked me about.

Day entered — Vessel, as the slate has it — Embers — Deduction — Banked to — Officer’s remark\par

Stone 12 — A man of the Weir. Birth-name not taken; entered as \emph{Eel} — 52 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Drawn before light. Pale round place left on the arm.\par

Stone 12 — A child three days returned, Low Kiln. Entered as \emph{Second} — 13, struck to 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Worse before dusk. Entered as a birth, not a worsening.\par

Stone 20 — A woman of the glaze room, High Kiln. Entered as \emph{Sweet} — 38 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Pale line at the gum. Asked after her girl; not entered.\par

Stone 20 — A clay-bound hand of the terraces. Entered as \emph{Seven} — 44 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Consent withheld. Clip-held by the wrist until consent entered.\par

Stone 22 — A man of Mud End. Entered as \emph{Peat} — 47 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Kiln’s breath. The neighbours called it merciful.\par

Stone 25 — A girl of the slip pits, Low Kiln. Entered as \emph{Nineteen} — 12 — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Birth-slate laid face down on the bench before the child was turned.\par

Stone 30 — A widow of the lower town. Entered as \emph{Loaf} — 41 — 1 in 12 — Greybank — Four loaves baked; three to the levy. Figure read twice, once for those that came late.\par

Stone 30 — Forty of Low Kiln. One slate for the batch, entered by lot — — — 1 in 12 — Hearthseat — Held overnight in the Waiting Room. Birth-names not taken. A barrow of grey went out through the north gate.\par

\subsection*{The column of embers}

An ember is said to be worth five marks and a newborn vessel holds twelve to fifteen. A labourer in good case carries forty to sixty and does not know it. The book does not ask what the walls are like; it asks only what went through them and where it was put. I have set the figures down as they were given. I have not added them, because adding is a thing the College does in the Hearthseat and not a thing a tally-clerk does at Greybank, and because the last time I added a column I got a number that would not agree with the printed one and the factor told me to copy the printed one again.

The officer gave me thirteen for the child on Stone 12. The factor’s clerk struck it and set twelve above in his own narrow hand, saying a vessel three days returned cannot hold thirteen after the draw. Both figures stand. I have asked which is right and neither of them has told me, and I have stopped asking, because a clerk who asks after a correction is a clerk who will soon be correcting next.

\subsection*{The remarks}

I struck out one of my own words on this leaf. Where the officer said \emph{the warmth was drawn}, I had written \emph{taken}, and he looked at the word and said a draw is not a taking when there is a slate. I set \emph{drawn} above and left \emph{taken} standing under it, which is the only honest thing on the page. A taking and a draw are the same heat going the same way; the slate is the difference, and the slate is a piece of stone with a neat hand on it.

The remarks are the only place in this book where a person appears, and even there they appear as a pale round place on an arm, a line at the gum, a word not entered, a wrist held until consent. The officer writes a good remark. He does not explain himself in them and does not plead. \emph{The neighbours called it merciful.} That is all he set down for the man of Mud End, and it is more than the ordinance would allow and less than a man would say.

\subsection*{What I did not enter}

The streak of slip in the gutter came off the forearms of a thrower who came in from Sill while I was copying the Stone 20 figures. She stood at the counter with her hands held away from her coat and waited for the figure, and the grey came off on the edge of the quire when she set her slate beside it. The green bead in the lower corner is not slip. It came from a girl who leaned over to see the writing with sweetness still at her mouth, and touched the paper and said nothing. I have left it where she put it. The drag of Ash along the foot was there when I opened the tin; it is not mine and not the factor’s clerk’s. I have not swept it. On the Last Day they sweep the corners of the houses and burn what they find there in the morning and call it dealt with. There is no Last Day for a tally-book.

One in twelve is printed on the notice and I have copied it eight times in these two tends. I have not checked it against the roll, and the officer has not asked me to. The figure goes into the book as it comes off the notice and out of the book into the Weighing, and a district hears it read in a clean voice and goes home knowing what it owes without having been told what it paid.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The factor’s clerk has written a line here that is not mine and is not in Ledgerhand:

\begin{quote}\itshape Nothing is lost that we have kept.\end{quote}

I have not struck it out. It is not a figure and has no business on a tally; but it is in the book now, and when I copy the leaf on Ilmen 1 I shall copy it again, in his hand and not my own, as it stands. The tin goes back on the shelf between the salt scales and the damp copies from the coast. The grey thumb will come off on the next leaf. I shall not rub that out either.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Eleven Weeks, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Keeping Concerning the Rising in Low Kiln and the Forty-One, with the List Set Against the Corners That Were Not Swept}
\CRsheetheading{The Eleven Weeks, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Keeping Concerning the Rising in Low Kiln and the Forty-One, with the List Set Against the Corners That Were Not Swept}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A chronicler’s extract from the annals of the Keeping, copied from a Hearthseat original; the year-entries in Ledgerhand, Pell Varr’s list entered as it stands, the answer of the hearth-maids kept in the margin, one song carried out of Low Kiln, and two hands of correction, one of which no hand will own · Written at the Hearthseat in the College of Assessors in Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by the keeper of the chronicle of the Keeping, who signs nothing and calls himself only the continuator; copied from an original of Y.H. 669 kept face down in the roll-room and carried forward at the Opening of the Slates into Y.H. 813. It survives as five leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the chronicle drawer under the narrow window that looks toward the Keel: an iron-gall thumb at the head, a soot print where a leaf was held too near the Hearth grate, a drip of tallow gone hard as a fingernail, slate dust in the gutter, a grey Ash print along the outer fold which the continuator did not make and will not sweep, one line struck through and written again underneath in his own hand, and one correction in the narrow upright hand of the College which takes the verbs out.\par}\medskip
I keep the chronicle of the Keeping, which is not the same thing as the chronicle of Grath. Grath writes what happened, when it can get a man to stand still long enough to ask. We write what was entered. Where the two disagree we set the entry down and leave the gap where it fell, because a chronicler who closes a gap has begun to write a sermon, and a sermon gets copied oftener than an account and lasts longer.

This chapter is the hardest in the book to copy, and not because of the figures. The figures are neat. It is the things that stand beside them that will not go into a year-entry, and so I have put them in the margin. A margin is the only place in a chronicle where a silence is allowed to stand.

\subsection*{The years as the roll-room has them}

\emph{Copied from the Hearthseat original, kept face down. The entries are in Ledgerhand. I have put the verbs back where I found them taken out and left the College’s hand standing above mine.}

\textbf{Y.H. 668.} In Low Kiln a levy was taken of ninety children’s warmth, for one whole return. No household in Sill could say whose return it was. There followed eleven weeks of disorder in the district, in the course of which the peace of the Keeping was disturbed and certain collectors were prevented from the discharge of their office. Entered as \emph{a disturbance of the peace}.

\textbf{Y.H. 669.} Assessor-Marshal Pell Varr came up from the Hearthseat with twelve collectors and a list. Forty-one persons dead, all of them spent in the keeping of the peace. The rising ended in the ninth week of his sitting. Entered as \emph{peace restored, account standing}.

\textbf{Y.H. 675.} Certain survivors of the rising first named in a Court file as being of the sealed opinion.

\textbf{Y.H. 683.} Quiet ash sold openly in the Hearthseat for the first time, by licence of the factor.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand of the College, against the first entry:} The levy was for a whole return. The return is entered at Greybank. Strike \emph{no household could say whose}.\end{quote}

I have not struck it. The return is entered at Greybank, which is true, and no household in Sill could say whose it was, which is also true, and the two truths have different shapes and must not be laid over one another. A man who writes the annals learns early that the word \emph{disturbance} costs less than the word \emph{children}. The word is chosen for the same reason a potter chooses a thin glaze, because it covers and because it is cheap.

\subsection*{The list}

Varr came with twelve collectors and a list. The list was the heavier thing he carried, and the only one he ever set down. It was made in the Hearthseat before he left, so that the names stood in a clean hand while the men who bore them were still going about their work in Low Kiln. This is not a cruelty. It is a method, and the method has a name in the College, which is \emph{economy of office}. I entered the words as they were spoken to me by a clerk who was present at the reading and has since been returned whole.

The list, as it stands in the roll-room, has four headings.

Heading — Number entered — What the heading covers\par

Persons taken for the whole return — 90 — Children of Low Kiln, entered under their houses\par

Collectors detailed to the district — 12 — Named, with their districts after them\par

Persons spent in the keeping of the peace — 41 — Named in the body of the report, not on the list\par

Weeks from the levy to the restoring of the peace — 11 — Entered as nine weeks sitting, plus two weeks travelling\par

Forty-one dead, all of them spent in the keeping of the peace. The phrase is exact, and it is the only phrase in these annals I have ever had to read twice to believe. A man spent in the keeping of the peace is a man who died while other men were being made to keep it. The College has weighed the phrase and finds it sound. I set it down as it came and have not tried to make it kinder.

There is one line in the report that I cannot place. It stands between the twelve names and the forty-one, in Varr’s own hand, and it reads \emph{and the corners also}. I asked three men of the College what the corners were, and got the same answer three times, which was that a corner is where two walls meet. This is true and is not an answer.

\subsection*{The corners that were not swept}

The hearth-maids of Low Kiln say nothing. I have tried four times to get it onto the page. Silence is not an entry, and the College takes verbs out of anything that is not one; in the end I wrote the only thing I could write, which is what the district does with the grey.

On the Last Day the ash in a Grath corner is left where it lies and burnt in the morning. That is the ordinance and the observance both. In the years after Y.H. 669, word came up from Sill that in the houses of Low Kiln the grey was not burnt in the morning either, but left in its ridge along the skirting board into Seed and past it. I could not get a man to say this before a witness. I asked a woman who had carried birth-slates in that district for thirty years and she gave me a date for answer, which is what they do when the thing asked for is not a date.

In the chronicle of the Keeping — What came up from Low Kiln\par

Forty-one spent in the keeping of the peace — Ninety taken, and no household paid them back\par

Eleven weeks of disorder — The kilns stood cold eleven weeks\par

Peace restored, account standing — The corners were not swept\par

The matter is closed — The grey is still there\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand of the College, against the third row of the right-hand column:} Corners are swept in due order on the morning after the Last Day. Enter as observance kept.\end{quote}

He has entered it as observance kept. Both rows stand. The ridge of Ash is the only entry in this chapter that cannot be corrected, because it is not a figure and not a word and has no verbs for him to take out. It is a grey line about two thumbs wide which turns the corner of a room without a break, and which somebody has to have put there, because Ash does not lay itself along a skirting board in the shape of a kept thing.

I set the hearth-maids’ answer in the margin rather than under the heading, because it is not an answer to the question the chronicle asks. The chronicle asks how many and when. They answer with a corner. It is the custom of that district to answer a number with an object, and an officer who does not know the custom goes away thinking he has been refused, when in fact he has been given the only true thing that was in the room.

\subsection*{The song out of Low Kiln}

\emph{Taken down from a woman of the drying racks who had not been in the district in Y.H. 668 and had learned the song from those who were. Sung low, at the washing, not at the fire.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Ninety went up in a grain-cart’s belly,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eleven weeks and the kilns stood cold;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve came up with a list in a clean hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the list had the names before they were told.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Forty-one spent in the keeping of the peace,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate says, in a hand that never shook;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners and four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one for the place where the ninety stood.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We do not sweep. We do not burn.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape We lay the grey where the promise fell.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Court has a word for the thing we keep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape we have a corner, and that serves as well.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Come back, come back, little pot of the clay,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the seam keeps the word that the mouth denied;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grey is not dirt and the corner is not dumb,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it holds the count that the slate would not hold.\end{quote}

The woman would not sing the last verse until the fire was banked, and would not say who made the song. I have left both things as I found them. A song that is sung at the washing and not at the fire is a song about work, and work is a thing a household can remember without being told to remember it, which is more than can be said of an entry.

\subsection*{The sealed opinion}

From the survivors of those eleven weeks came the people the Court calls Unbanked. They call themselves nothing at all, which is a hard thing for an office to enter, and the College has entered it as \emph{refusal of designation}. Their argument is old and I have set it down once, plainly, because it is the only part of this chapter that the chronicle has had to make room for: if the world must be kept, let it be kept perfectly, so that nothing leaks, nothing is owed, and no one can give anything away. A world of unbreakable vessels would be a world of the walking dead. That is their saying, not mine. The Court’s public answer is that they are mad, and the answer is entered in the Weighing notices, where the figure one in twelve is also printed.

The Court’s private answer is in a sealed file in this building, two rooms from where I write. I have not opened it and am not likely to be asked to. There are doors in the Hearthseat that a chronicler passes every day and is never required to go through, and a man who keeps the annals learns to measure a room by the doors it has as well as by the walls.

In Y.H. 683 quiet ash was sold openly here for the first time. I am old enough to have seen the first phial go over the counter and to have known the woman it was for. I have not put her name in the entry. She paid in marks, which is a thing anyone can write down, and with something she said at the counter, which is not.

\subsection*{What the College hand did}

Where I wrote of the ninety children that they were taken and not returned, a narrower hand set \emph{the account stands} above and left mine under it, in the manner that takes a verb for a thing a man might smuggle in a cuff. Where I wrote \emph{the corners were not swept}, it wrote \emph{observance kept}. Where I wrote that Pell Varr came with a list already made, it wrote \emph{precautions taken}. It is a careful hand and a clean one, and it has never once in this chapter changed a figure.

There is a line at the foot in a hand I do not know, struck through twice and written again underneath, and it says: \emph{They took the warmth and left the account, and the account is the only thing that came back whole.} I have copied it as it stands. The hand that wrote it wanted to be found and did not want to be known, which is the state of most hands that write in the margin of this book.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The iron-gall at the head is mine; a chronicler who keeps a quire open through a tend marks himself before he marks the page. The soot came off the grate on a night when the Hearth was low and I held a leaf too near to read it. The hard drop of tallow is from the lamp in the roll-room and has been there since the first copy. The slate dust in the gutter came off a surveyor come up from Keld who leaned over my table with the Rim still on his cuffs and would not sit down. The grey along the outer fold is not mine and is not the College’s. I have had this leaf four years and have never swept it, and if the factor asks me why a chronicler leaves dirt on a chronicle I shall tell him it is entered as observance kept, which is a phrase he will accept without looking up.

The leaves go back into the drawer. The annals go on, as annals do, and next tend I copy the quay tallies from Greybank and after that the Weighing figures. The ninety have no row in the figures and the corners have no heading, but the grey turns the corner without a break and the levy is still read at one in twelve in every Court room in Sarn. I have put both down where they stand. A chronicler does not settle a thing by writing it. He keeps the place where it stood, so that the next hand has something to copy besides the clean version.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Line of Figures and the Line of Squares, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Cantons}
\CRsheetheading{The Line of Figures and the Line of Squares, Being an Extract from the Chronicle of the Cantons}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} An annalist’s extract from the chronicle of the Keeping, being the account of the Empty Cantons; copied from a Hearthseat original and set beside a surveyor’s field note, a Fen song, and two hands of correction in the margin · Written at Greybank in the factor’s house in the last tend of Stone, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, and copied forward at the Opening of the Slates in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, by the keeper of the annals there (the office stands on the roll, the hand does not); copied from an original kept face down in the roll-room of the Hearthseat. It survives as four leaves of foolscap sewn with wire into a board cover, kept in the annals drawer beside the winter tallies: a brown iron-gall thumb at the head, slate dust in the gutter, a tar print from the quay along the fore-edge, a dried Fen reed folded between the second and third leaves, a small square of bare paper where a word was scraped away, one correction in the narrow hand of a clerk of the College and one in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I keep the annals in the factor’s house at Greybank. The office stands on the roll and the hand does not; when the factor wants a name for the hand he writes \emph{the roll-room}, which is as much a name as a man with no house is allowed to have. What follows I copied in the last tend of Stone, in the Thin Year, from an original kept face down in the Hearthseat, because the man who set it there did not care to have it read standing up. I have put verbs back where I found them taken out. A chronicle with no verbs in it is a thing a man can read aloud in a clean voice and go home believing, and I have had to stand at this table and listen to too many clean voices.

The Empty Cantons lie sixty leagues south of Sill, between Grath and the Fenmarch, on no road a cart can make in a day. A man can walk into them, and several have, and come back with nothing to tell except the lie of the ground. There are roads still rutted where no wheel has gone in eight hundred years; wells with the stones laid tidy about them and the water down out of sight; doorways standing where the walls have gone; and in every third doorway a square of bare clay where something used to hang. The Fen reeves call the place the Quiet Acre. The Court calls it the Empty Cantons. The temple calls it nothing at all, and that is how a place is made to disappear.

\subsection*{The account as it stands in the roll-room}

\emph{Copied from the Hearthseat original, Title the First, Of the Cantons Beyond the South Road. The figures are in Ledgerhand. The squares are in the original; I have set the word square within them so that no copyist fills them with a nought.}

Year — Hearth-fires — Souls on the roll — Embers entered — Whole returns\par

Y.H. 1 — 1,204 — 6,110 — — — —\par

Y.H. 3 — 1,204 — 6,106 — 36 — 6\par

Y.H. 12 — 1,198 — 6,088 — 192 — 41\par

Y.H. 40 — 1,190 — 6,061 — 240 — 60\par

Y.H. 41 — square — square — square — square\par

Y.H. 100 — square — square — square — square\par

Y.H. 418 — square — square — square — square\par

Y.H. 812 — square — square — square — square\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow hand of a clerk of the College, against the five rows of squares:} Squares are not entries. Enter as nil.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{Underneath, in mine:} A square is where a figure stood and was taken away; a nought is a figure put in its place. He has put noughts in the squares and the column balances. That is how I know it does not.\end{quote}

The figure the College likes is six whole returns in the third year after the lighting, which is the year the first Returns were recorded and the year the roll begins to have something in it worth counting. I have not checked the addition of that column, and I have learned not to. The last time a clerk of this office added a column he got a number that would not agree with the printed one, and the factor told him to copy the printed one again, in a better hand.

\subsection*{What the temple tells the children}

The temple tells it this way. The Cantons were taken up in the first Returns, and their people are whole somewhere, though no record says where. The cost of those first whole returns was entered against a province, and the province is this one. I set that down because it is written in the roll-room and not because I can say what it means. A chronicler who explains a figure has begun to write a sermon, and a sermon is a thing that gets copied more often than an account.

The oldest ledger says only that the fires went out in a season of no frost. The words \emph{returned elsewhere} were added by a hand that writes with its verbs taken out, and every copy since has been smoother than the one before. I have set the smooth words under the rough ones and left both standing. When the temple voice reads them at a Weighing it makes a mercy of a line of squares, and a household hears a mercy and goes home, which is the whole art of that voice.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In a hand I take to be a temple hand, struck through} went out in a season of no frost \emph{and written above,} were gathered into the Hearth. \emph{Both stand. A hand that strikes a thing out and writes above it is a hand that wants the thing gone and cannot bear to lose the place where it was.}\end{quote}

\subsection*{What the ground keeps}

Three surveyors have walked the Cantons that I know of. Two went for the Court and one went for the Keldish, and none put his name to the account, which is the first thing the three accounts agree on.

The river road is there under the turf, rutted to the depth of a cart’s wheel. The wells are dry but not fallen in, and the stones are laid round them in the old order, which a man does not do when he is leaving in a hurry. In the doorways the squares of bare clay are where the house-rolls hung, and not one of them has a nail in it now. In one doorway a slate still stands in its notch. The figures on it are not figures a clerk of this office can read, and the Vorr, being asked, said that the numbers were correct, which is an answer a man can carry away and still know nothing. The deepest marks were not cut with iron. The surveyors of Keld have one word for such marks and the Court’s copy has another; I have written both in the margin and chosen neither, because a chronicler who chooses between two guesses has made a fact of one of them and will have to answer for it.

The hearths are cold, and the ash in them is not grey. This is the thing the surveyors set down last and speak of least. A hearth that has been used has grey in it, and a hearth that has never been used has none; these have a white dust like bone meal, and no fire has ever been in them that any man can find. A man of the Fenmarch told me the white is what is left when a promise has been kept too long. I have not put that in the account, because I do not know it for a lie and I do not know it for the truth, and the annals are not the place for a thing I cannot weigh.

\subsection*{The song the reed-cutters carry}

\emph{Sung on the marsh road going in, not coming back. I took it down from a reeve of the Standing Post who would not sing it while a man in a clean coat stood on the boardwalk.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Sixty leagues and never a smoke,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the wells give down and the doorways stand;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the reeve counts ruts and the ruts count back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and nobody lives in the quiet land.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Four for the corners and four for the wall,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a square where the name of the house should be;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the fox has the hearth and the reed has the well,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the slate in the door keeps a figure for me.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape They went up in the thaw and came not in the ice;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the Court has a figure for how many went,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a square for the ones the figure forgot,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the square is the only one I have spent.\end{quote}

The reeve said the last line was about the song and not about the Cantons, and when I asked him what the difference was he said a man who needed the difference explained would not have sung it. I have copied the line as it came and put no gloss on it.

\subsection*{The matter of the fifth spring}

In Y.H. 618 the Court sealed a fifth of the Nine Wells and hanged the keeper of it for drawing without a key. The roll gives the office and not the name, which is the Court’s way of hanging a man twice. The Fen reeves say the spring that was sealed is not under the Keel at all but under the Cantons, and that the Court’s survey puts it twenty leagues from the Hearthseat so that no collector need walk the south road. I have copied their saying and the Court’s figure side by side. One of them is a place and one of them is a number, and a chronicler who joins the two is drawing a map, which is a thing I have no licence to make.

\subsection*{What was struck out, and what I did not}

Where I wrote \emph{who paid for the sixty empty fires}, a narrower hand set \emph{the account stands} above and left mine under it, saying a chronicle is not a slate and need not be argued with. I have kept both. A question that a clerk can answer in four words is a question that has been answered already, and not by me.

In the margin of the third leaf a hand I do not know has copied a sentence, struck through twice and written again underneath: \emph{Another kept badly, and we inherited the crack.} I have seen the same words on the back of a slate that came out of the Old Kiln and lies now in a kiln-house in Low Kiln, where nobody knows what it is. The man who copied them here wanted them found and wanted them not to count, which is the state of most things in this office that matter. I asked a Vorr who came through Greybank on the Hearth Road what the words meant. He said the numbers were correct. I asked a man of Keld and he turned the slate face down and said he had not seen it.

\subsection*{At the foot}

The brown thumb at the head is mine; iron-gall will mark a man who keeps a quire open through a tend, and there is no washing it out of the creases. The slate dust in the gutter came off a surveyor who leaned over my table with the south-road dirt still on his cuffs, and he would not sit down. The tar along the fore-edge is from the quay, where I set the leaves while a barge unloaded salt and I counted a carter’s figures and let my own leaf take the weather. The reed between the second and third leaves was put there by the reeve who sang; he folded it the way a man folds a thing he means to come back for. The small square of bare paper is where I scraped a word away with a knife and put no other in its place. It is the only square in this quire that I made myself, and I made it deliberately, which is more than I can say for the others.

The leaves go back into the drawer at Greybank. At the Opening of the Slates I copied them again and put the squares in again with my own hand, because a square is the only figure the Court has never learned to read. The Cantons have no people and no smoke, but they have roads, and a road is a thing somebody meant to come back along. The annals go on. Next tend I copy the quay tallies, and after that the Weighing figures from the Hearthseat, and the squares will keep their places in the roll for as long as there is a hand to set them there.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sermon at the Flat Stone, Being What Was Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 812, with the Old Words Left in Knots Because Fen Cant Will Not Write}
\CRsheetheading{The Sermon at the Flat Stone, Being What Was Said Over the Traps on Ilmen 15 of Y.H. 812, with the Old Words Left in Knots Because Fen Cant Will Not Write}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A sermon of the Weir preached at the blessing stone on the north bank at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill; the saying in Grathic, the three old lines held in the margin as knots of grey wool, with the tally-keeper’s corrections, a Court clerk’s in Ledgerhand, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Preached at the Fish Blessing by an old woman of the Weir who had stood at the stone at thirty blessings, over the traps lifted and set on their sides on the plank walk, on Ilmen 15, Y.H. 812, the Thin Year; written that evening by a woman of the Weir who keeps the eel tally and has no slate-name, on the back of a weigh-slip spoiled by a wet figure out of Greybank, and sewn with eel-sinew into the folded reed wrapper that holds the knot-accounts in the Eel House. It survives with a salt crust at the head where a flat hand was set to brush the grit from the cut, a silt tideline along the gutter from a morning the plank walk stood under water, eel slime on the second leaf, a fish-hook nick nobody will own, a grey Ash print from a cuff at the stone, three knots left over right with the tail under against the three old lines, and a fourth knot tied through a hole in the first leaf for a word the preacher would not give out. Copied once at Greybank in Silt, Y.H. 812, and again in Ilmen, Y.H. 813, with the verbs put back and the knots left as they were tied.\par}\medskip
I keep the eel tally at the Weir and nobody asked me for this. I write because the old woman’s words went into the water and the water kept them, and I wanted something on dry paper that a clerk could not carry away in a cuff. She stood on the flat stone with her sleeves salt to the elbow and spoke to the stone, the traps, the river, and last of all to us, which is the order the women of this place use when there is work to be done and somebody may be listening who wants a figure. I have set down what she said in Grathic. The three old lines are not Grathic and are not written anywhere; I have tied three knots in the margin against them, left over right with the tail under, which is how we keep a thing here that we cannot spell.

The salt crust at the head came off her hand when she flattened it on the stone to brush the grit from the cut. The silt tideline along the gutter is from the morning the plank walk stood under water and I carried the leaf under my apron. The eel slime is mine: I set the leaf down on the bench to count and a fish came out of the basket onto it, which the old woman called a blessing, and I did not argue. The fish-hook nick is not mine and I don’t know whose. The grey print came off a cuff at the stone and nobody will own it; I have not swept it. The knot through the hole in the first leaf is the fourth, and I tied it for the word she would not give out.

\subsection*{The order of the blessing, as the stone actually has it}

\emph{Written small, from watching, not from any order the Court has printed.}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Brush the stone free of grit so the cut shows. Do not ask what the cut is. It was here before the tally and it will be here after.

\item Stand with your sleeves damp and salt in the creases of your hands. Salt on the stone and along the weir head, with a flat hand. Not on the traps. The traps have their own business.
