A pot is honest. I have set a pot down on this bench for twenty years and known by the sound of it what it would do. I have never known a man that way, and I have stopped wanting to. The lime takes the print of a hand and keeps it after the hand has gone, which is a trick the Court would like if it had thought of it.

\subsection*{The water}

\begin{quote}\itshape The Ferr comes down with the dust of the west,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape cold in the throat and sweet in the sleep;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three hundred went thin on a stream with no name\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the Court wrote the figure and called it a war.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape It ran then as it runs now, downhill and cold,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the women of High Kiln drank it for years;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape White hands, full cup, and the rest goes round.\end{quote}

My mother was of High Kiln and she would not let me drink the Ferr, which I thought was a novelty of hers and am now old enough to know was a judgment. She never said why. When the physicians came down from Greybank in the year the sweetness was written about, she let them look at her gums and gave them a cup of barley water and sent them back up the road with nothing they wanted. She died thin but not sweet, and I have kept that as a thing to be careful with rather than a thing to be proud of.

\subsection*{The verse they do not sing before a man from Greybank}

They take this one up when the clerk has gone back down the road with his satchel under his arm. I have it from the bank-man, with the space left before it, which is the space they leave in the singing.

\begin{quote}\itshape One in twelve, says the notice, read twice at the Cross;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the cart counts four and the kiln gives back one;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one that is left is the one at the bench\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape where a man sat down and did not get up.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The cup goes round and the cup comes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the name goes up and the name comes down;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Lift to the stone; it outlasts the name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place at the end of the bench stays set.\end{quote}

I asked the bank-man whose bench it was. He said every bench in Stonemouth has an end, and went to see to the kiln. There is a man who used to sit there whose name I still take for an ale on the tend’s last day and still give back when the factor’s man comes. I have not entered him anywhere else. A name kept in a room is a different weight from a name kept on a slate, and I have found that a woman can carry the one when the men beside her have put the other down.

\subsection*{What the face-man wrote in the margin}

Against the verse about the Ferr, a man who has worked the face for thirty years wrote in a hand that shakes at the ends of words:

\begin{quote}\itshape Two of mine went thin on that water. The slate says none. I have put the two where a clerk can see them if he ever looks away from his paper.\end{quote}

He brought me the leaf himself and stood at the door while I read it, and took it back to the face without a word about the ale he had not been given. I have kept his two in the margin where he set them. The room has never once sung that verse with the two in it, and the men know it is there.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The clerk come up from Greybank borrowed the leaf on a market morning, being a man who cannot leave paper alone. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He struck out \emph{it outlasts the name} and set above it, \emph{the measure is recorded and the residue nil}. Against the lime he wrote \emph{entered in kind}, which is a true figure and a cold one. Against \emph{three hundred went thin} he wrote \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, and numbered the lines from one to four so that a man could read them without singing. Where the lift stands he put a small square rule and wrote \emph{no vacancy in the roll}. He took the verbs out of two lines as though a verb were a thing a man could carry off in a cuff and sell at the next crossing.

I have put the words back underneath his and left his standing above. He can enter the lime in kind; the kiln has given back the same weight for twenty years and nobody has disputed it. He can enter the stream as a war, because there is a war on a slate somewhere and it saves a man the trouble of looking at the water. What he cannot enter is the place at the end of the bench, and he has not tried. A clerk knows the difference between a figure and a place better than a woman who keeps a room has any right to, and he has made his living on it.

He scraped a word off the lower leaf and would not say which. I have left the bare square where it stood. A word can be taken off paper; the space it leaves is harder, because the paper remembers where it was and the eye keeps going back to it. This is the whole of the account between this room and Greybank, and neither of us has settled it.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The lime at the head came off my own cuff when I held the leaf down in the draught under the door, and it has worked into the grain where nothing will get it out. The blue-grey along the fold is the Ferr: a man came in from the weir head with wet sleeves and set his cup on the leaf while he was telling the bank-man something about the upstream water, and the tell was lost when the water dried and the blue stayed. The ring is mine, from a cup I set down before the first question and took up after the last, which is how this house measures a conversation. The tallow is off the lamp I kept low while I wrote, so that the men at the table would not know I was writing and change the words for me. The grit in the gutter is coarse sandstone and came out of a boot, not a pocket; no man in this room carries stone away, and I have never asked the boot. The grey along the outer fold came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying. I have not swept it. There is no Last Day in a cracked pot behind a door.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape The bench keeps a place and the cup keeps a ring;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the stone knows the both and says neither thing.\end{quote}

I asked the room whose it was and had three answers and no hand, as I have had before about the grey print and the scraped word. I have set it down as it stands. The leaf goes back into the cracked pot behind the door, and tomorrow the draw comes again and the men lift to the stone, which does not answer and asks nothing of anybody, and the place at the end of the bench stays set.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Twelve and the Dish, Being the Counting Rhyme of the Low Kiln Children, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, and What a Clerk Made of It}
\CRsheetheading{Twelve and the Dish, Being the Counting Rhyme of the Low Kiln Children, with the Counting-Out, the Manner of the Turns, and What a Clerk Made of It}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A hearth-maid’s gathering of a children’s hopping game, set down in Grathic on the back of a spoiled Weighing notice; the verses in the children’s own half-sung speech, the rules in the hearth-maid’s small careful hand, a correction in the narrow upright Ledgerhand of a factor’s clerk borrowed at Greybank, a gloss pressed into the margin by a woman who has kept the birth-slates for nineteen years, and one line at the foot in a child’s grey chalk · Set down at the birth-flower shrine in Low Kiln of Sill in Stone of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, of an evening when the yard stood frozen and the children hopped the trodden-ash floor of a kiln-house two doors down the Clay Yard; carried to Greybank in the satchel of a hearth-maid come to have a widow’s mark confirmed and copied onto the back of a Weighing notice gone soft at one corner. Kept folded in the shrine’s slate-box among the birth-slates that have been answered. It survives with slip worked into the grain at the head, a green bead of lead-glaze in the fold, a tallow thumb at the second corner, a grey Ash print along the gutter that nobody will own, a tideline where the notice went damp, a twist of grey wool through a hole in the first leaf which the writer will not untie, the clerk’s correction standing above the children’s words, the birth-slate woman’s gloss in the margin, and a line of grey chalk at the foot in a hand that has learned its letters off a slate and will not be claimed\par}\medskip
I keep the birth-slates at the shrine and I have written this because a man from Slate Row stood in the yard and asked what the children said when they jumped. He wanted a figure. I told him there was a count in it and no figure, which is the truth of the thing, and he went away and sent me a clerk instead. What is below is what the children said before the clerk came, and what they said again after he had gone back over the north bridge. I have set the clerk’s hand above mine where he put it, and the children’s words under it where they stand, as the floor keeps the ash and the foot that raised it.

They play it in Stone when the yard will not bear a foot, on the trodden-ash floor of a kiln-house where the fire is banked and the boards hold a little warmth. They play it in the thaw as well, on the dry boards under the racks, and not during the Five, because in the Five the children are made to stand and listen and there is no floor for it. Some twist a plait of grey wool and call it the eel and hold it between two hands; the words are the same words and the twelfth is the same twelfth. A mother will tell them not to knot the wool, because a knot of grey wool is an account and a child who ties one in play will be asked what it counts.

\subsection*{The counting-out, said before the floor is taken}

\emph{Right fists held out, knuckles up. The child who says it points at each fist in turn and does not look at the faces. The fist it lights on at the last word keeps the crack, which is to say she draws the line on the floor and calls the fault. She does not get to hop first. She is the one who has to be fair, which the children accept as a punishment and the rest of the yard accepts as practice.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Crock and dish and crock and dish,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the potter’s thumb and the eel’s wish;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape pit and rack and wheel and sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the one it lights on keeps the crack.\end{quote}

\emph{Say it to the floor. Said looking at a child, it becomes an argument, and there is always a child who will argue.}

\subsection*{The rhyme, as it is hopped}

\emph{One line, one hop. The line drawn in slip or in the grey is thumb-wide and must be crossed, never touched. A child who touches it has gone wrong and sits on the ash at the edge of the floor while the others go around her. At the twelfth line the hopper must cross twice without setting a foot down between; that second crossing is the dish, and the kept one. If she puts a foot down between, she is banked and sits with her arms folded until she is brought back. The last thing said before they stop is the bringing back: three children say her name, and she comes in again. A child whom nobody brings back is thin until the next round. The children will not be told why the twelfth is the kept one. If you ask them they say it is the dish, and if you ask what is in the dish they ask you why a man wants to know what is in a dish.}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the pit where the slip comes up,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape two for the bench and the hollow seat,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the rack where the wet ones stand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the crack that you must not meet.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Five for the thumb on the birth-slate’s rim,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape six for the grey where the skirting turns,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape seven for the bell that wants one more,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eight for the eel that goes in and stays.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nine for the step that comes back askew,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ten for the broom that goes around,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape eleven for the word we say at home,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape twelve for the dish, and the one kept out.\end{quote}

\subsection*{A note on the several hands in it}

The fifth line is not mine. I wrote \emph{the thumb on the birth-slate’s rim} because that is where the hand goes at a birth, and a woman beside me at the shrine put her mark in the margin against it and wrote, \emph{not the thumb on the rim — the thumb over the writing}. It is Alda Reed’s hand, I think, though she has never said so. She crossed two fingers over a child’s birth-flower on the seventh day of Stone and would not say the word for it, and she has kept her own account of this game in her head for nineteen years without once setting it down. Her reading is better than mine. A hand on the rim is a hand that might lift the slate; a hand over the writing is a hand that has already decided what the slate will say. I have left both lines standing, hers in the margin and mine underneath, as a kept thing is left where it fell.

\subsection*{What the clerk did}

The factor’s clerk borrowed the leaf at Greybank, being a man who cannot let paper lie. He has a cuff gone soft from washing and the ink sits in two fingers of it and will not come out. He numbered the twelve lines in the margin, struck through \emph{the one kept out} and wrote above it, \emph{the deduction is one in twelfths, the residue is nil, the young are instructed}. Against \emph{twelve for the dish} he wrote \emph{the twelfth is retained for the Hearth}. At the foot of the count he put a round nought and wrote \emph{absence} beside it, where the children’s game ends with a name said three times.

I have put their words back underneath and left his standing above. He takes the verbs out because a thing always true has no need of them. I put them back because a child up to her ankle in the grey of the yard does not know she is hearing something always true, and wants to know which foot to lift. A nought is a number. The dish is a place at the table. He has put a figure where a place should be, which is the whole art of that hand.

He asked me what the children learned from it. I told him the count and the fault and the bringing back, and he said that was an account of the Return taught before the child could read a slate, and he entered it. The children stop when a man in a soft cuff comes into the yard. They take it up again when he is past the bridge, and they never once change the twelfth.

\subsection*{The verse they do not say while a man from Slate Row is in the square}

\begin{quote}\itshape One for the lean and two for the thin,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape three for the loaves that go on the dish;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the slate says one and the yard says none,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the name said at home is the only one.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape The dish goes round and the dish comes back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and what was kept is counted as lack;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape four for the corners and one for the sill,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the place where the twelfth stood is standing still.\end{quote}

I have it from the child who keeps the crack, with the proper space left before it, which is the space they leave in the hopping. She would not say it while the clerk had his pen out, and would not say it to him at all. She said it to the floor with her back turned and made me put it down as I have it, with none of my verbs in it, because a verse said to the floor wants nothing added, and a verse said to a man wants everything taken away.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The slip at the head is off the hand that drew the line; it goes into the grain and will not come out, which is why the yard uses it to mark a place. The green bead came off a pot broken in the glaze room and rolled as far as the fold before anybody saw it. The tallow thumb is mine: I held the notice down in the draught under the shrine door and did not know I had marked it. The grey in the gutter came off a cuff laid where no cuff has business lying; I have not swept it and there is no Last Day in a slate-box. The tideline took two words off the back of the notice and I have not written them in again, because a rhyme with two words gone is a rhyme said slowly, and all of ours are said slowly. The twist of grey wool through the hole is mine, tied for the word I could not put down. I will not untie it.

\subsection*{At the foot, in grey chalk, in a child’s hand}

\begin{quote}\itshape I kept the crack and nobody came.\end{quote}

No hand will own it. The letters are set down as they were made, hard at the \emph{th} and one of them backward, which is how a child writes who has learned off a slate and not off a book. I asked whose it was and had three answers and no hand, as I did with the grey print. I have left it where it was written.

The leaf goes back into the slate-box with the birth-slates that have been answered. Tomorrow the yard will draw its line again, and one in twelve will be read in a clean voice at the notice-board, and the twelfth will be kept out of the count and brought back at the end of it, which is more than can be said for the district’s own twelfth. The children will go on saying the name three times. I have kept their words and I have not joined them to anything.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Cold Keeps, Being an Account of the Country Beyond the Cold Pass}
\CRsheetheading{What the Cold Keeps, Being an Account of the Country Beyond the Cold Pass}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A quarryman’s itinerary and travel account, set down on the back of a spoiled Keldish survey sheet and a strip of birch bark; part road-log, part inventory of what came back, part complaint, with the corrections of a Court survey-clerk in Ledgerhand, a Keldish surveyor’s note in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 811 at Keld Keep, on the Rim Road and beyond the Cold Pass, by Orrel of Stonemouth, a quarryman who went west as a hired guide to a survey party and came back down the Rim Road in Seed of Y.H. 812 with a stone in his pocket, one year gone by the slate and three by his face, and no memory of the debt he went to recover. Copied at Greybank in Ilmen of Y.H. 813 onto the back of a discarded tally-roll, sewn with wire into a fold of oiled sailcloth and carried in a tin. It survives with coal dust ground into the head, a smear of hot lead at the fold that has burnt through one word, a crust of white frost along the gutter, a single white hair pressed between the second and third leaves, a small grey stone folded into the gutter, one correction in the narrow upright hand of a Court survey-clerk, one note in the broad slow hand of the Keldish surveyor who borrowed the leaves, and a line at the foot in a hand nobody will own.\par}\medskip
I went west to recover a debt and came back with a stone. The debt had a name on it when I left and no name when I returned, and I have left the place where the name stood rather than put a figure in it. A figure would stand. I have seen what stands and what does not out there, and I am not the man to say which of the two is true.

I am a quarryman of Stonemouth. I cut lime and coarse sandstone out of the bank where the Ferr comes down, and I know the weight of a stone by the hand before I know it by the eye. In Seed of Y.H. 811 a surveyor come through the village hired me to carry instruments and guide a party up the Rim Road, and there was a debt between us that I thought a man could collect if he walked far enough behind it. This is the account I kept. I have set down what happened and what did not, and where the two disagree I have left both standing, which is a thing a clerk cannot do and a quarryman can, because stone does not care which of your accounts it lies under.

\subsection*{The road as far as the last pass}

From Sill to Keld Keep is a hundred and twenty leagues of improving road and worsening weather. Only fools and factors travel it without a warm-stone. I went with one in a fold of wool against my belly and another in the cart, and I do not say now who paid for the second, because I have asked and the answer comes back in a voice I do not recognise.

At Keld Keep a man states his measure before he states his name. I stated mine and was told it was a lowland figure and would not carry me ten leagues beyond the pass, which was true: it did not. The survey-clerk who hired me wrote this down in the margin as a kindness, since it cost him nothing. In that city a man’s number is cut into his forearm at thirteen and cut out again when he comes back thin, and I saw three men with smooth places on their arms where a number had been, and I saw a fourth who had had his changed twice and could not say which of the two he had been born to. None of them asked me my name. All of them asked my measure. This is a difference a Grath man notices and does not enjoy noticing.

Ten leagues beyond the Keep the road goes through the Cold Pass, which Karric VII shut in Y.H. 741 and the agreement of Y.H. 747 fixed as the border. There is a survey post there and no gate. The Warden’s surveyors do not promise to bring a man back, and this also was written down, in the same hand. I asked the clerk whether a promise not made was a promise kept, and he said that was a question for a lowland moot, and went on writing.

Past the last pass no map is honest. I carried that sentence out of Keld and set it here because it was the only true thing anybody told me in that country. The survey party turned back at the post. I went on, because the debt was on that side and because a man who has come a hundred and thirty leagues to collect a thing is a fool in exactly the way that keeps him walking.

\subsection*{The country itself}

There is no weather in the Waste. Weather is a change, and the cold there does not change. It is not a great cold, the way Stone is cold in Sill; it is an even, patient cold that has nowhere to go and all the time in the world to get there. A man does not freeze in it so much as come gradually to agree with it.

The Keeping teaches that the Waste is the sink where everything unheld goes. I have no quarrel with that; a man who has worked a quarry knows about sinks. What the Keeping does not teach is that a sink is a country, and a country has people in it, and those people have no use for a slate. There is nothing to count out there. No ember changes hands, no mark is made, no collector comes with his iron tube and his clean figure. The Court has never opened an account beyond the pass, which is the only mercy in this world that costs the Court nothing.

They say the cold is not empty. They say it is full of what nobody kept. I have no reason to disbelieve them and several to believe them, and one of those reasons is in my pocket.

\subsection*{The people, and what they give}

The bands beyond the Rim are called Wastelings. They have no banks, no Returns and no word for a debt. They are not the Unbanked the Court speaks of, who have a design and a name and people to argue with; they are simply the spent. A man there owns what he is still carrying and nothing else, which makes for a short inventory and a long silence.

They leave their dead sitting upright facing the way they came. They do not cover them. I asked why, and a woman who had stood beside one for a morning said that a man who had come that far had a right to be seen off in the direction he had travelled, and that covering him would be a sort of argument with him, and they did not argue with the dead. I set that down as she said it. A Grathic hearth-maid would have covered the body with a fold and crossed two fingers and given me a date. Both acts are kindnesses. I have never seen two kindnesses so unlike and so complete.

A Wasteling will give a stone, or a name, or a day’s warmth, and expect nothing back. This stopped me longer than anything else in that country, because in Stonemouth a gift that expects nothing is the one thing a man cannot enter, and a thing a man cannot enter is a thing he cannot afford. I took the stone. I have not entered it. The woman who gave it to me wanted nothing, and I still do not know what to do with that.

Ask a Wasteling what he fears and he will ask whether you are warm. At first I took this for evasion. On the ninth day I understood it was the whole of his information, and the only question worth asking a man who has come that far.

\subsection*{The ninth day}

I went out with a porter of Keld who had opened a way in his forearm and had the numbers cut out and put in again twice. He was a man of few sentences and those all about the road. On the ninth morning out he stood close to my little fire, closer than a man stands to warm himself, and I thought he was warming himself. He was not warming himself.

The Keldish call such a shape a cold-eater. It stands close to a vessel and draws its Warm away; it takes and does not give. There was no struggle and no sound. In the afternoon his fingers were the colour of skimmed milk gone off, and by the third watch he had forgotten his numbers, and by morning he had forgotten that he had ever had a name. We did not say the thing’s name aloud, because a name gives a thing a place in an account, and there is no account out there.

The cost is the part the books leave out. I carried one warm-stone out and brought two back, and one of them is his. I have not given it to anybody because there is nobody to give it to, and because if I set it down I should have to say what it cost. It sits in the gutter of this account where a figure should be, and the Clerk has been at it, as you will see.

\subsection*{A song they sing at the sitting-down}

\emph{Set down in Grathic letters from the mouth of the woman who gave the stone. The last line is said three times, and the third time is for the one who cannot say it.}

\begin{quote}\itshape Beyond the last pass there is no weather,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape no mark, no debt, no name to spend;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the dead sit facing the way they came\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and the cold keeps what nobody kept.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape A stone for a stone and a name for a name,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and a day’s warmth for whoever can carry it;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape ask me what I fear and I will ask you this:\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape are you warm? are you warm? are you warm?\end{quote}

I asked her what the third asking was for. She said it was for the child who had not yet learned to be cold, and that a child could not answer and the question was asked anyway, which is the way the world treats a child. I have left that in, though a clerk would take it out.

\subsection*{What went out and what came back}

Went out with — Came back with\par

One warm-stone in a fold of wool — Two stones; the second is not mine and I have not entered it\par

A clay cup out of the meal mill at Sill — A cup, cold, that answers flat when set down, and nobody to tap it\par

A slate with a name and a debt on it — The same slate, one year older, with the name gone and a figure in another hand\par

A porter of Keld with numbers on his forearm — A man with a smooth arm who answered to no number and went on walking\par

A year by the slate, Seed of Y.H. 811 to Seed of Y.H. 812 — Three years by my face, and a morning I cannot account for\par

A debt to collect — A stone to keep\par

There is a place in this table where a line should stand and does not. I have set the stone in it. If you hold the leaf to the lamp you can feel the stone through the paper, which is more than I can say for the figure.

\subsection*{What the Clerk did}

A survey-clerk of the Court borrowed the leaves at Greybank. He struck out \emph{the cold keeps what nobody kept} and set above it, \emph{The measure is retained in the Waste.} Against the second warm-stone he wrote \emph{no value entered.} Where I had left the place where the porter’s name stood, he put a round nought and wrote \emph{vacancy} under it.

Against the debt he set a figure and wrote \emph{satisfied} beside it. It is the only satisfaction I have ever been given that I did not receive. I have left his hand standing and mine under it, the way a quarry leaves the spoil above the stone.

\subsection*{From the man who hired me}

At the foot of the second leaf, in the broad slow hand of the Keldish surveyor, who borrowed the leaves before the Clerk did and returned them with the fold changed:

\begin{quote}\itshape The numbers are correct.\end{quote}

He was asked, beyond the post, to translate a marking cut in a stone that was not cut with iron. He gave that answer and turned the slate face down. I asked him twice and got the same words both times. In Keld that is an answer a man can carry away and learn nothing from, and it is the sort of answer that keeps. I have set it where he wrote it and added nothing.

\subsection*{At the head and in the gutter}

The coal dust at the head came off the surveyor’s cuff in the lamp-room at Keld Keep; he leaned over my sheet and would not sit down. The hot lead at the fold came from a sample wrapped in the same paper. It has burnt a small hole clean through the word \emph{pass}, and I have not written the word in again, because a hole in that word is the honest state of it.

The frost-crust in the gutter came up out of the paper on the ninth morning, when I carried the leaves inside my coat and the coat froze to my chest. The white hair is not mine and is not the porter’s; it lay pressed between the leaves when I found them in the snow, and I have kept it there. The small grey stone is the one I came back with; I have folded it into the gutter so that the account and the thing it accounts for travel together. The grey print along the outer fold is not mine. There is no Last Day out there and nothing gets swept.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape A man is a vessel set down facing the way he came.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Nobody covers him, and the cold does not lose him.\end{quote}

I asked the woman who gave the stone, the survey-clerk and a factor come up from Greybank, and had three answers and no hand. I have left the line where it was written. The leaves go back in the tin, and the tin goes under the bench at Stonemouth where I keep the things I cannot enter. If I am asked what I went for I shall say a debt, because that is the word I was taught. If I am asked what I brought back I shall say a stone, and put my hand in my pocket to feel it, as I have done every morning since Seed of Y.H. 812.

\clearpage\phantomsection\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{What the Dog Ate, Being a Grave-Guard’s Field Notes on the Bone-Hound at the Greybank Burial Grounds}
\CRsheetheading{What the Dog Ate, Being a Grave-Guard’s Field Notes on the Bone-Hound at the Greybank Burial Grounds}
{\centering\FellFont\itshape\footnotesize\color{faded} A soldier’s field book on one beast, set down as the record of a watch and not as natural philosophy; the rounds in Grathic, the tally in charcoal on the back of a spoiled granary docket, a digger’s song in the words it is sung, the factor’s clerk’s corrections in Ledgerhand in the margin, and one line at the foot in a hand nobody will own · Written in Bone and Ash of Y.H. 812, the Thin Year, by Watt of Greybank, one of the factor’s men paid by the tend to keep the south-bank burial ground; set down at the end of watches in the watch-hut with a tallow end in a pot, first on three dry grain-dockets from the Court’s granaries and then on the back of a weigh-slip gone soft at one corner, sewn with eel-sinew and carried in a coat pocket. Copied forward in Ilmen of Y.H. 813. It survives with a grey Ash thumb ground into the head, a brown spot the size of a fingernail where a man’s blood fell on the second leaf, a wet boot-print across the foot from a morning crossing the ford, a nick from a billhook at the fore-edge, the charcoal rubbed thin where the leaf was carried, two corrections in the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, and the one line at the foot\par}\medskip
I keep the south ground at Greybank for the factor. It is not a post a man boasts of. The dead laid there are mostly such as came back thin out of the district, and they go into shallow clay with a potsherd at the head and no slate read aloud over them. My work is to see that they are not opened twice. Once is the hearth-maids and the diggers; the second is somebody else, and it is the second I am paid to stand against. I carry a billhook and a short spear with the head gone grey on the quay stone, and I write this at the end of a watch with a tallow end in a pot and the cold coming up through the soles of my boots.

The grey thumb at the head is Ash. I have tried to knock it off and it went into the fibre. That is what Ash does. There is nothing mysterious in it, except that a man who has never held a pot over a room where a promise was not kept will call it dirt and be done with it.

\subsection*{The ground}

The ground lies south of the town beyond the Ilm, a short way past the winter ford, and in Stone you may cross on the ice if you know where the ice is sound. There are two sorts of grave. The old ones are long and set in rows with a headboard gone soft at the foot. The new ones are small and close under the south fence, dug by Mott, who is paid by the grave and not by the hour, so that he has an interest in their being shallow. I have no quarrel with him. A deep grave in this clay costs a man his winter.

What I noticed first, and wrote down before I knew what to call it, is that the new small graves do not take the frost like the old ones. On a morning in Bone I laid the back of my hand on six mounds in the row. Four were cold clay and two had a little softness under the crust, the way a banked coal is soft under its skin of grey. I have no name for that and I have set no cause beside it. Mott says it is warmth rising off the river. The diggers say the clay was turned late. Both may be true. I have kept the shape of it, which is the only work a watchman has.

\subsection*{What comes}

It is a dog. I will set that down first, because the hearths will not. It has a dog’s teeth, a dog’s neck, a dog’s way of putting its head on one side when it listens, and the long narrow muzzle of a dog that has been fed out of a ditch. It is bigger than the yard hounds at the Tallow Works and thinner. Its coat is the colour of wet clay and carries no grey on the outside; the grey is in the mouth and under the nails, and a man who has opened one will know where I mean.

It comes out of the low ground south of the fence in the second watch, which is when the tallow in the hut is down to a knuckle and the men on the quay have stopped shouting at one another. It does not bark. The diggers have a song about the barking which is wrong in every particular, and I have set the song down below with the wrong part standing, because a thing sung wrong for twenty years is part of the ground as much as the graves are.

It does not attack a man. I have stood within two paces of one with my spear down and it went on with its work and never looked at me. But put a man between it and a grave it has chosen and it will bite. That is the whole rule, and there is no courage in testing it twice.

\subsection*{The bite}

Mott put his foot in a hole at Ash 5 and came down on one knee with his hand in the clay, and the dog was already there. I struck it across the back with the spear-shaft. It went away three paces and stood, which is what it does; it does not run off and it does not come back at a man who has hit it. Mott’s bite was two small holes on the thumb-side of the hand, grey at the edges, and not much blood. We washed with salt and water and bound it. At the end of the tend it was still open, with the grey where the edges had been.

Salt does not hold that bite. The physician at Greybank told Mott to keep it warm, which is what physicians say when they have nothing else to say, and Mott kept it warm and the hand went on being a hand with a hole in it. He has a rag on it now and will not show it at the market. I put the size of the holes in the margin because a man cannot close his hand and I have had to watch him try. The clerk has written over them, which I did not ask him to do.

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand of the factor’s clerk, written along the margin:} Wound: not entered. No deduction arises.\end{quote}

I have left his hand standing. A clerk’s hand is an iron thing and has its use: it keeps a man from arguing with what he cannot change.

\subsection*{The song}

Sung by the diggers going out to the south ground in the dark, not coming back. The second line is their error and not mine. I have not corrected it, because Mott sings it loudest and would take it ill.

\begin{quote}\itshape Two for the big and three for the small,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it barks at the wall and it comes to the wall;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape it puts its nose to the new-turned ground\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and takes what the ground has not yet made cold.\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape \end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape Count them going and count them back,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape a horn for the reeve and a phial for the jar;\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape the grey in the mouth and the grey on the hand,\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\itshape and one that is kept and not entered.\end{quote}

\subsection*{The tally}

These are the nights I kept a true account of. There were others I did not write because my hands were full and one I did not write because I had drunk. I have set down both sorts as they stand. The figure in the last column is mine, not the clerk’s.

Night — Place — Opened — Grey gathered — Lost\par

Bone 4 — Small row, south fence — one — one — none\par

Bone 13 — Small row, west end — two — one — none; wind off the river\par

Bone 22 — Old grave under the alder — none — none — spear lost in the clay\par

Ash 5 — Small row, third mound — one — one — Mott’s hand\par

Ash 16 — Two graves, the old ground — two — two — none\par

Ash 27 — New ground beyond the fence — three — one — dog stood and did not go\par

\begin{quote}\itshape \emph{In the narrow upright hand:} Openings: six. Loss of property: nil. No entry arises.\end{quote}

There is no property in a grave, so he is right, and he has written \emph{nil} where I wrote Mott’s hand. I have set my line under his and left both where they fell, the way a digger leaves the clay on top of the pot and knows what is underneath it.

\subsection*{The jar and the horn}

There is a man comes up the south road at the dusk of Account-day with a jar under his coat and no horse. He is of the fen people and speaks little. He pays five bits a phial and asks no questions, which is the price of quiet ash in the Fenmarch and the reason a man asks no questions at it. I do not know what dog it was that gave the grey, and I have never asked him what house will buy it. I have held the jar while he filled it from the thing we scrape out of the beast when one is taken. I have never taken the bits. A man may say that and still know it is not enough.

The horns go a different way. A reeve of the Standing Post came in Frost and paid two bits a horn, and the horns went south to be cut into count-sticks. I asked him what a stick counts that a slate cannot. He said a stick cannot be read by a man who is not standing over it, which seemed to him a virtue and to me a great deal of trouble. But the diggers like them. Mott keeps one in his belt and turns it when he is deciding which row to open, and it has more notches than there are graves, which I have not asked him to explain.

\subsection*{What the hearths say}

The hearths say the dog guards the graves. I have stood and watched it go to the small new ones first and pass the old ones by, and I have seen what it leaves in the clay. A thing that guards is not a thing that eats; but those are words too fine for me, and I have written only the order in which it went. From the south fence to the third mound, then the west end, then the old rows if the watch is long and the tallow is low. That is the whole of what I know. I have not written why.

\subsection*{At the head and in the margins}

The Ash thumb at the head is mine; I held the docket down in the draught that comes under the watch-hut door and did not know I had marked it. The brown spot on the second leaf fell there from Mott’s hand when he sat down to have the rag changed, and I have not scraped it, because it is the only entry on this leaf that cost anybody anything. The boot-print across the foot came off the morning I crossed the ford after the ice went thin and came up to the calf in silt; it has dried into the grain and will not rub out. The nick at the fore-edge is the billhook, from the night the dog stood at Ash 27 and I struck at it and missed. The charcoal is rubbed thin where I carried the leaf in my pocket against my thigh. The clerk’s two lines I have not touched. The song is as the diggers sang it, barking and all.

\subsection*{At the foot, in a hand nobody will own}

\begin{quote}\itshape What goes into the ground is kept by somebody else. Ask the jar.\end{quote}

There is new low ground beyond the south fence that I have not walked, and the dog comes out of it with clay on its chest that is not the clay of these graves. I will go in next Bone with a fresh spear and Mott’s counting-stick, and I will count them going and count them back, and if the grey comes from a grave nobody laid I will set that down too, in my own hand, with the verb left in it.

\chapter*{The Reckoning of Days}
\markboth{The Reckoning of Days}{The Reckoning of Days}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{The Reckoning of Days}
\begin{CRtimeline}
\CRday{Day 1}{Stone 7, Y.H. 812 (Seventhday)  —  the birth room off the Clay Yard in Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Corin is born two hours old with Daniel Marchetti’s whole memory and a branching red flower on his ribs; the stone Dessa warmed at the Vail fire goes cold at his belly while a name is entered in a neat dark hand on Alda’s slate before anyone has looked at his face, Mira gives bread and keeps her back to the writing, and Sella’s door-burned hand feels for the warmth, hovers over the bundle and withdraws with the third day still to come.}
\CRday{Day 2}{Stone 8, Y.H. 812 (Eighthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and wheel-shed, and the birth room of House Silt, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  In the kiln-house the fire keeps its four-and-four-and-a-gap breath around Garl’s hollow wheel-seat, salt coat and unswept Ash ridge while Tarn pockets and returns the bench knife and Jorra declares the foundling is not Vail to a Sella who answers the pot instead, and three doors down Corin, two days old, hears the flat note of a cup he cannot reach, feels the warmed stone go past temperature, endures Alda’s ordered washing and unasked-for dates and Des’s laugh from a Chicago car park, while Dessa calls her cough weather, counts nineteen steps and refuses his name as the room arranges an unspoken question about who pays to keep him.}
\CRday{Day 3}{Stone 9, Y.H. 812 (Ninthday)  —  the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house with its wheel-shed and Debt Loft, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Sella carries the covered bundle up the icy yard with the burn-door closing on its weight and the boy counting her steps, while Dessa stands at the end of nineteen steps she does not take with her thumb on the sieve-wire scar and Alda tells her he went in the levy among the children taken for the account and lets unasked-for dates settle over an unspoken figure, leaving the cold stone behind on the abandoned bed, and under the Vail roof the boy is laid on fresh straw with heat returning painfully to his hands and feet, hears Jorra’s sentence sealed and Tarn’s I’m-a-debt-not-a-foundling and a second flat note from a pot, and sees the charred edge of a slate in the kiln ash that he cannot reach, the market and the Cross still ahead.}
\CRday{Day 4}{Stone 10, Y.H. 812 (Tenthday)  —  the Clay Yard, the Cross and the Slate Row end of the market, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; one remembered Cook County trauma bay  —  Sella Vail carries the boy in a basket under wool from the banked Vail kiln to Account-day at the Cross, where Berr Clay wipes his thumb on his apron and reads one in twelve, as the notice says, twice to two hundred leaning people while the boy counts a hundred and nine steps, eight pigs and the market bell’s four-four-and-a-gap and hears the slate give its flat answer a third and a fourth time; Ostrowski’s voice breaks through in the present tense with the two duties and a pocket with no phone in it, a clerk’s neat hand with its small stop is seen a third time, Berr confirms Sella’s widow’s mark at Greybank as a kindness entered while leaving Garl’s tile debt uncalled, Alda Reed crosses two fingers at the flower and covers the sign with a date, Mira Silt asks her own eel price without once looking at the basket and shoves a loose board clear, Ash goes out in a barrow toward the north gate and the Bone Orchard, and Sella turns back up the yard with the boy holding numbers he cannot spend and a note he cannot place.}
\CRday{Day 5}{Stone 11, Y.H. 812 (Firstday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and wheel-shed, the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Under coals that held all night Sella Vail touched the widow’s mark before she opened the kiln and at no other time while the five-day-old boy could not keep wool on his chin and she put the fold right without looking, Tarn took the small bench knife, set it back where it could be checked and stopped his broom two strokes at a Vail pot’s flat note without turning his head, Jorra spoke to the pots with slip dried to old bone on his forearms, and Alda Reed came under the roof to give a neighbour mother exact dates over a rekindled child going grey and wrote a note she turned writing-down, leaving the boy with cold, hunger and a sound nobody in the house named.}
\CRday{Day 6}{Stone 12, Y.H. 812 (Secondday, the Hearth Drawing)  —  the Vail kiln-house, a neighbour’s death-house two doors down, the threshold of House Silt, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; two sentences in a remembered Cook County bay  —  Sella carried the boy in the basket to a neighbour’s house and set him at the edge of the light where a collector with a soft cuff took a cold iron tube to a dying man’s arm and the man gave with the small flat knock --- fifth hearing of the note and first from a person --- while the figure read at the Cross was entered in a neat ordinary hand as the account stood, and later the rekindled child was worse on the third day of its return, Alda turned a second note down under a milk cup, the death-house Ash ridge measured a finger’s width thicker than the ridge at Vail and turned the corner without a break, and the year’s first measure had been taken from the dying and the newly born on the same day before Sella banked the coals at dusk, fed the boy from the house’s own dish and passed Dessa Silt counting nineteen steps into her thumb at her threshold without a look into the basket.}
\CRday{Day 7}{Stone 13, Y.H. 812 (Thirdday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Sella Vail touched the widow’s mark before she opened the kiln and at no other time and fed the seven-day-old boy barley gruel from the house’s own dish while a pot on the shed bench was turned toward before it was set down and gave nothing, the interval kept as an object and the hearing count still five from four sources, while Tarn, the knife already back on its sill, saw the turning and stopped his broom half a stroke at the empty set-down and said nothing, Jorra worked the wheel with bone-pale slip and no slate dust, the number of days to Kindling went around as a closed fist and entered the house as an absence, Tarn’s sixth year was counted and his seventh held back, and at dusk Sella banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark.}
\CRday{Day 8}{Stone 14, Y.H. 812 (Fourthday)  —  the Fishstairs below the north bridge, the row up from the Ilm and the walk back to the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; two remembered sentences in a Cook County cafeteria  —  Sella carried the eight-day-old boy down before light to buy eels, where Mira Silt worked with pale slime on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, flicked eel-bones while deciding whether to lie, gave Berr Clay four eels where six should go against his two marks short for six years, called the basket warm off the slate and not on one, and touched the grey cord at her waist when a figure was spoken, while a collector crossed the bridge with a soft cuff and two present-tense sentences of a cafeteria at four in the morning and a paper wrapper eaten to its last crumb broke through and were taken back by the river, and the boy counted four steps down and four and a landing where a step should have been before Sella bought two pair of eels and carried him home with the bucket swinging at her knee and river silt on the wool.}
\CRday{Day 9}{Stone 15, Y.H. 812 (Fifthday)  —  the edge of the fish-trade in the north bridge’s shade, the Fishstairs, and the Vail kiln-house at dusk, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Sella set the nine-day-old boy in a patch of shade no slate had reached, where Dessa Silt stood at the end of nineteen steps with slip-grey nails, a sieve-wire scar and the cough from the pits called weather, counted four loaves on the seventh of Stone and bits to the woman with a basket, and did not look in, while a green-mouthed girl watched the pots and Mira’s grey cord lay at her waist over a second cord never taken to Nine Pots before she put a brown-edged barley crust into the fold --- a crust, not a sermon --- that he could smell and feel but could not lift to his mouth, and at dusk Sella counted her loaves twice, Tarn put the small knife back on the sill and Jorra moved the damper, leaving the boy on his bed under the roof with the warmth at his side and his hand going up an inch and coming down, four, four and a gap.}
\CRday{Day 10}{Stone 16, Y.H. 812 (Sixthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Ten days old with the market crust gone cold in the fold, the boy watched Sella Vail touch the widow’s mark before she opened the kiln and at no other hour, measured the kindling stack with Tarn as four bundles and four and a space where the fifth should be while Sella arranged her loaves so the days to Kindling stood as a shape no collector could enter, heard Jorra say \emph{you’ll do} to a pot in bone-pale slip and move the damper before she had finished, and lay under Alda Reed’s hand as she reached for her slate before she reached for him, touched the tin once inside her bodice, crossed two fingers at the red edge of his wrist without knowing it and covered the sign with an unasked-for date before writing a note she turned face-down into her shawl and went on giving dates after the question had stopped.}
\CRday{Day 11}{Stone 17, Y.H. 812 (Seventhday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Tarn swept before light, set the small bench knife back on its sill and announced it to the empty yard, went still for two breaths when Sella said he had done well, then agreed flatly and swept on, while a pot turned toward on the bench gave nothing and his broom stopped half a stroke at the empty set-down and neither he nor the boy named the second interval, and Sella called the kiln’s breath the danger a man slept into in Mud End and the district called that death merciful, Tarn held the pale ring at his left wrist up to the light and put the knife back where it could be checked, and Jorra shifted the damper with no slate dust on his forearms and did not say the back room was cold.}
\CRday{Day 12}{Stone 18, Y.H. 812 (Eighthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, the Clay Yard and the yard well, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The figure of the days went around the yards shut in a fist and arrived under the Vail roof only as an absence, and a neighbour at the threshold spoke around Garl’s uncalled tile debt while Sella kept her half-pace and said \emph{the house} where another woman would say I, and at the yard well another neighbour reached for her slate before her child and for two sentences the boy was in a ceiling light at four with a chart’s note turned face-down and a hand going past it to a signature, then in a pocket that held wool where a lit phone with a name had lain, and the hand came back with nothing as he filed it beside the other record-first hands and found wool, woodsmoke and the cold crust at the end of the reaching.}
\CRday{Day 13}{Stone 19, Y.H. 812 (Ninthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and the yard path toward the Ilm, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  A man come up from the river with water frozen on his legs held a shard of ice to the tallow light in which a dark hair ran and stopped a thumb’s breadth short of the edge, a woman from High Kiln said the thaw would come early and everybody who wanted it late contradicted her because a late thaw puts off what is payable in the thaw, a neighbour back from the Court’s room described its bench by the door, pot, draught and gap which the boy set beside the birth room and the death-house without joining them, and Sella measured the Ash by a thumb’s width --- near two thumbs here and a finger more two doors down --- leaving both ridges to turn their corners unbroken until the Last Day while the household kept its number badly and he kept it exactly and could spend neither.}
\CRday{Day 14}{Stone 20, Y.H. 812 (Tenthday, Account-day)  —  the Cross, the Court’s table at its Slate Row fringe, and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Sella carried the fourteen-day-old boy down in the basket and set him in the moot-post’s shade a half-pace from every open slate, where the bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself, Berr Clay wiped his thumb and read one in twelve to two hundred leaning people, called the levy for the feast and said it was not called by him, went around the uncalled tile debt and did not look into the basket, and a soft-cuffed clerk at the Court’s table laid his hand on the top slate before he looked at the woman waiting and said it stood as entered, while the boy saw the small pause in the neat dark hand a fourth time --- flare, birth-slate, Cross on Stone 10, now here --- unread and unjoined to the other three, with the Drawing collector’s ordinary hand kept apart, and at dusk the coals hissed under ash, the fold was put right, the crust stayed cold in the fold and the Five were eleven days off.}
\CRday{Day 15}{Stone 21, Y.H. 812 (Firstday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The last tend opened with Sella Vail touching the widow’s mark before she lifted the lid and at no other hour, fuel and bread counted into the days in loaves, glances and one brown-edged loaf set apart while the boy carried his own exact number down to the kindling stack standing four, four and a space where the fifth should be, somebody back from looking at the ice bringing a number in a shut fist that was called a cold and answered with the fire, and Jorra working in bone-coloured slip with no dust, moving the damper early, while the kiln breathed four, four and a gap and the crust lay cold in the fold.}
\CRday{Day 16}{Stone 22, Y.H. 812 (Secondday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and a neighbour’s house two doors down, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Tarn swept before light, set the small knife on its sill, told the empty yard it could be checked and said to the kindling six counted and the next he did not count, then fetched a collector for a neighbour whose cuffs were soft from washing and fingertips the colour of skimmed milk gone off and who set his hand to the slate before the bed saying the measure was taken and the account stood as entered, while on the way back a carried vessel gave its flat note past the door and Tarn’s head turned a degree and under the roof the boy filed the half-heard note with the intervals, not among the five hearings from four sources.}
\CRday{Day 17}{Stone 23, Y.H. 812 (Thirdday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed and the drying racks, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  After five clean mornings Jorra Vail came in with fine grey slate dust worked into the creases of his forearms past the bend of his little finger, said nothing of where he had been, told the wheel it did not care whose hands only if they were steady and went to the damper before Sella had finished, while low talk in the back room and missing slates under the drying racks stood only as shapes with a door kept shut, Sella got quieter and the yard straightened around it, and the boy filed the dust beside the ridge, the charred slate and the barrow of grey and made nothing of the likeness.}
\CRday{Day 18}{Stone 24, Y.H. 812 (Fourthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Alda Reed came under the roof smelling of soap and warm milk, laid the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turned to the basket, touched the little tin inside her bodice once without opening it, pressed the fold too long, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower without knowing it and covered the sign with a date nobody had asked for, went on giving exact dates after the question had stopped, said warm and breathing which was exact and not true, and wrote on a narrow slate what she did not leave lying about, turning it face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy could not name.}
\CRday{Day 19}{Stone 25, Y.H. 812 (Fifthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The cold came down another degree with oiled paper lifting at the windows and a grey skin on the Slip Brook, Sella set the basket facing the kiln wall to keep the river wind off his ears, and two paces from his head a pot cracked all the way through with the small flat knock he knew and nobody called a sound, which he could not turn toward, so a woman called it a pot gone wrong and he filed it as a third object on the interval tray while Tarn’s broom checked half a stroke at the place and said nothing, Jorra’s forearms were clean of dust, and the warmth crossed into him at the bank and was entered nowhere.}
\CRday{Day 20}{Stone 26, Y.H. 812 (Sixthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, the Clay Yard and the yard well, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  An ordinary Sixthday and not Account-day passed with mending, drying, sweeping and eating, while the number for the Five went around the yards in mouths and fists as three, then two, then whatever the moot gave out, a neighbour at the well counting it twice and a third saying it would be whatever the moot gave out before the argument ended in weather, Sella rearranged her loaves and fed him gruel thinned with milk with the warmth entered nowhere, Tarn swept twice and replaced the knife on its sill, and the boy kept the one number none of them would give, that one day after tonight was tomorrow.}
\CRday{Day 21}{Stone 27, Y.H. 812 (Seventhday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and the drying racks, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  A woman from High Kiln with sweetish lead-glaze at one corner of her mouth said the thaw would come early and neighbours who wanted it late contradicted her because the levy fell in the thaw and Tarn said to the thatch that late was his and meant a longer week before the paying, ice-mice spread through the thatch and a numb grey patch on a child’s hand was called what the cold did, the boy kept the thaw argument and the hairline in the ice together and drew no line between them, and the kiln breathed four, four and a gap while the district’s figure and the fire’s figure did not agree.}
\CRday{Day 22}{Stone 28, Y.H. 812 (Eighthday)  —  the Clay Yard, the yard well and House Silt three doors down, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Mira Silt came up from the eels with silt on her sleeves and the top of her left ear gone, answered a question with a question and her own answer, put her thumb under her apron to the grey cord when a figure was spoken, gave a fresh brown-edged crust briskly into the fold saying it was a crust not a sermon, and showed a second cord twisted twice under her belt that had never gone upriver to Nine Pots, while three doors down Dessa coughed from the pits at the end of nineteen steps, called it weather, counted nineteen out and nineteen back and four loaves on the seventh of Stone in eight hundred and twelve, smoothed her sieve-wire scar and shut her door-shut smile without looking into the basket, leaving the old crust cold beside the new.}
\CRday{Day 23}{Stone 29, Y.H. 812 (Ninthday)  —  the Clay Yard, the Vail kiln-house and a neighbour’s house two doors down, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The yard made ready for the Last Day with brooms and a date said aloud two or three times, a woman said the grey would be left where it lay until the Last Day and burned the morning after and called dealt with, Sella laid one thumb into the Vail ridge and then the death-house ridge a finger’s width thicker without saying which was which, Garl’s salt coat kept its shape on its peg and the uncalled tile debt went around in a careful circle, Tarn offered to check the width with his thumb and set the knife on its sill, Jorra went quieter with no dust on his forearms and would not say the full note was in a Vail pot before it left the wheel, and at the bank Sella did not touch the mark.}
\CRday{Day 24}{Stone 30, Y.H. 812 (Tenthday, Account-day)  —  the Cross, the Court’s table at its Slate Row fringe, the market’s edge and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Sella carried the twenty-four-day-old boy down in the basket and set him in the moot-post’s shade with cold iron at his cheek and both crusts in the fold, where the bell went four, four and a gap, Berr Clay wiped his thumb twice and read one in twelve as the notice says, said the levy was called for the feast and not by him and did not look into the basket, the district gave the Five out as three days off, a soft-cuffed clerk at the Court’s table laid his hand on the top slate before looking at the woman waiting and said it stood as entered, and the small pause in the neat dark hand came a fifth time without joining the other four, with one untagged beat of orange flare light on wet snow in which a hand in a grey sleeve found wool where a lit rectangle with a name had lain and the name was not looked at, before Sella carried him home at dusk, banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, the fire keeping four, four and a gap and Kindling tomorrow.}
\CRday{Day 25}{Kindling, Y.H. 812  —  the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Before first light a coal under ash came up the yard in a clay dish from hearth to hearth with its source and cost unspoken, Sella Vail touched the widow’s mark once before tipping it into the kiln and fed the twenty-five-day-old boy from the house’s own dish without wiping his mouth, and he counted the new firelight four, four and an empty shelf where a fifth would be while a collector’s first measure of the year went into a shut fist and a woman’s thought-better-of sentence, the coat, hollow seat, unbroken ridge and charred slate keeping their places and the two crusts lying uneaten in the fold.}
\CRday{Day 26}{Weighing, Y.H. 812  —  the outer fringe of the Cross, the doorway of the Court’s room and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  An officer read the year’s measures in a clean voice wearing a temple’s clothes and announced a whole return for somebody not in the yard with a name the household would not repeat, Berr Clay wiped his thumb at the edge of the reading with his red cord folded under his coat and went off with his box still locked, and the boy set the silence after the name among the gaps while the Court’s room came to him only as a voice through a doorway with a bench, a pot, a draught and a missing line, which he laid beside three other rooms without writing a cause.}
\CRday{Day 27}{the Long Night, Y.H. 812  —  the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  With no fire relit after dusk the house sat in the dark telling of the Return --- a thin child who knew warmth before a face, a man returned with somebody else’s hands, Alda Reed’s dates standing where wonder should have stood --- while the boy counted the gaps between voices and kept a told bell of four, four and a gap beside but never on the heard bell, cold arriving at cheek, temple and wrist with neither breast nor crust given, Tarn holding his seventh year back and Jorra saying nothing of the back room.}
\CRday{Day 28}{the Remembering, Y.H. 812  —  the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Names went from door to door along the yard but not one under the Vail roof, where Sella went around Garl’s unspoken name as around ash left in a corner and the boy filed the silence where it should stand with the other gaps, Alda Reed laid birth-slates on the bench, touched her tin unopened, crossed two fingers at the birth-flower without knowing it and covered the sign with a date while in the old register a hand found wool where a lit rectangle with a name had lain and the name went unlooked-at, the charred slate and the two crusts staying where they lay.}
\CRday{Day 29}{the Last Day, Y.H. 812  —  the Vail kiln-house, the Clay Yard and a neighbour’s house two doors down, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Bread was baked with no third crust for the fold, Mira Silt came up from the eels to answer a question with a question and her own answer, touched the grey cord under her apron at a figure and showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it without any knot counted, and Sella would not let the ash be swept early, laid one thumb into the Vail ridge and the same thumb into the neighbour’s a finger’s width thicker, left both turning their corners unbroken, and banked the coals without touching the mark.}
\CRday{Day 30}{Ilmen 1, Y.H. 813 (Firstday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The grey left where it lay was burned before light and called gone and dealt with while the coals stayed banked and the mark untouched for want of an opening, Slate Row was spoken of as a direction with one in twelve printed and unchallenged and the true deduction unspoken, work turned toward the thaw and the slip pits while the Ilm held under its ice, and the thirty-day-old boy carried his count --- five hearings from four sources and no sixth, the empty fifth, the unspoken name, five pauses unjoined --- into a year the district had already entered, his hand going up an inch toward the warmth and coming down.}
\CRday{Day 31}{Ilmen 2, Y.H. 813 (Secondday)  —  the yard well, the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  A woman let down a bucket and said the water tasted different while a man come up from the Ilm said the ice was honeyed under the mud and nobody said the word for it, the oiled paper sagged and the Slip Brook lost its stiff skin behind the racks while a warm spell became the weather, and the thirty-one-day-old boy in the basket kept the shape of what a district could taste and would not name while Mira Silt answered a question with a question and put her thumb to a grey cord with a second twisted twice beneath it, neither counted, and his hand outside the wool went up an inch toward the bucket and came down.}
\CRday{Day 32}{Ilmen 3, Y.H. 813 (Thirdday)  —  the Vail kiln-house and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The boy was a month old and nothing marked it while Tarn set the small knife on its sill and told the yard it could be checked with six years of seven counted and the seventh held back, agreed with everything so thoroughly that no argument could stand and wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying, Sella fed him gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish and said the house where another woman would say I, his broom checked half a stroke at the place where no note had come and Ash came up the colour of the clean dark line when he scraped his knuckles, the proverb went to the pot and the coals were banked without a touch of the mark.}
\CRday{Day 33}{Ilmen 4, Y.H. 813 (Fourthday)  —  the Vail wheel-shed, the drying racks and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Jorra Vail came in from the back room with fine grey slate dust worked into the creases past his bent little finger and said nothing about where he had been, told a pot it wanted thinner slip and the wheel it did not care whose hands only if they were steady and went to the damper before Sella had finished, the men whose names are not spoken stayed unnamed and the space under the rack where whole slate should have stood went around by everybody and entered by nobody while the boy kept grey-dust forearms and clean-slip forearms on separate trays and a pot set on the bench was filed with the objects that were not hearings, the count still five from four sources.}
\CRday{Day 34}{Ilmen 5, Y.H. 813 (Fifthday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Alda Reed came smelling of soap and warm milk and laid the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, gave a date where a wonder should have stood, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower without knowing it and covered the sign with the same unasked-for date before going on with dates after the question had stopped, wrote a fourth hidden note in the second hand and turned it face-down toward a floorboard the boy could not name, and said warm and breathing, which was exact and not true, while three doors down a cough was called weather.}
\CRday{Day 35}{Ilmen 6, Y.H. 813 (Sixthday)  —  the drying racks, the Clay Yard and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  A pot set down out of a woman’s shadow answered nearly full under nobody’s knuckle with a thumb’s breadth of air under the note and a want in it, the first earthly answer to the interval carried since Stone 13, filed on its own tray advanced and not paid and not added to the five hearings from four sources, Tarn’s head went a degree toward it and he swept on without naming it, Jorra told the pot it would do and moved the damper early, Sella touched the widow’s mark before she opened the kiln and at no other hour, and the boy kept the missing breath, the empty fifth in the carried firelight and the nearly full note in three separate places with a hand outside the wool that went up an inch and came down.}
\CRday{Day 36}{Ilmen 7, Y.H. 813 (Seventhday)  —  the yard well, the edge of the Ilm and the Clay Yard, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The ice showed a hairline running in and stopping a thumb’s breadth short of the edge, carried into the thaw from the shard held to tallow on Stone 19 and set beside the missing step at the Fishstairs and the told bell in three places, a man came back with a figure in his fist and thought better of giving it so the number went around as a shape nobody gave out, Berr Clay wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing, had a number he did not care to give and went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked while the Singing Sill’s low note and the thaw itself were called weather, one in twelve stood printed and unchallenged, Tarn agreed with both sides and kept his seventh year held back, and at dusk the coals went under blind ash without a touch of the mark.}
\CRday{Day 37}{Ilmen 8, Y.H. 813 (Eighthday)  —  House Silt three doors down, the Slip Brook and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Sella set the basket in the shade of the nineteen steps where Dessa Silt stood with her shoulder against the jamb, slip-grey nails and wet clay at her hem, her cough worse than on Stone 28 and still called weather, put nineteen out and nineteen back into her thumb, counted four loaves on the seventh of Stone in eight hundred and twelve with three to the levy and bits to the woman with a basket, drew her thumb over the sieve-wire scar and did not look into the basket or say the number or the name, Mira passed her sister without looking and brought no crust, the Slip Brook ran clay-heavy a little higher than it should, and when Dessa’s thumb went to the wicker for one breath an old hand in a grey sleeve reached for a pocket and found wool with a boat on cold water unsaid, the boy carried up the yard at dusk thirty-seven days old with the two crusts in the fold and his hand going up an inch toward the warmth and coming down.}
\CRday{Day 38}{Ilmen 9, Y.H. 813 (Ninthday)  —  the Slip Brook behind the drying racks, the Fishstairs and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The clay-heavy rise came up in the night and took Dessa Silt from the end of nineteen steps, and the yard lifted her out with their hands and no words while the thirty-eight-day-old boy, held on the bank, heard the small flat knock of a body cracked all the way through --- the sixth hearing of the full note and the second from a person, beside the five from four sources and not among them --- and kept the paid shape of her thumb on the wicker, Alda Reed coming after the vessel had given to reach for her slate before the body and lay dates where a wonder should have stood, a soft-cuffed clerk set at the Fishstairs for a measure nobody had called for, and the two crusts waiting in the fold at dusk.}
\CRday{Day 39}{Ilmen 10, Y.H. 813 (Tenthday)  —  the Cross, the moot-post’s shade and Slate Row, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Account-day resumed over a woman uncollected in the brook, Berr Clay wiping his thumb twice and reading one in twelve as the notice says before taking himself out of his own sentence while the true subtraction went over the basket, the number for the thaw passing from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and never arriving, a soft-cuffed clerk’s hand going to the top slate before his eyes went to the woman waiting, and the boy keeping his exact count of four ways out of the square and the bell’s four, four and a gap with nobody crossing himself, the fold put right at his ear without a look at his face.}
\CRday{Day 40}{Ilmen 11, Y.H. 813 (Firstday)  —  the Vail kiln-house, the drying racks and the yard well, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  No collector came for the woman in the brook and nobody found a word for the omission, so warmth could be left where it fell and the morning came anyway while the bucket went round without a slate, Sella measured the clean dark line where the Ash turned against the death-house ridge by a thumb and left both where they lay, Tarn set the knife on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back and swept the road to a collector without turning because a late thaw puts off the paying, Jorra’s bone-coloured forearms went to the damper ahead of his hand, and Sella fed the boy barley gruel from the house’s own dish and touched neither crust.}
\CRday{Day 41}{Ilmen 12, Y.H. 813 (Secondday)  —  the Fishstairs and the Slip Brook behind the drying racks, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Mira Silt came up from the eels with pale slime on her sleeves and her head held to the right where the top of her left ear had been, answered a question with her own answer, put her thumb to the grey cord when a figure was spoken and showed the second cord twisted twice beneath it with neither knot counted nor door lifted, brought no third crust and did not look into the basket, while the weir women’s talk of the blessing and its number ended in weather and the Slip Brook ran clay-heavy behind the racks, kept with the honeyed ice and the hairline in three places.}
\CRday{Day 42}{Ilmen 13, Y.H. 813 (Thirdday)  —  House Silt three doors down and the Vail kiln-house, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Sella carried a clay jar three doors down and set the basket just inside a door standing a finger’s width open, where the boy saw from the height at which shelves are highest a round pewter tin above the empty bed with a pale fold at its seam and a thumb’s bright rub on the lid and entered it nowhere, nobody said the woman’s name or the number in her thumb, and Sella opened no slate and turned no fetching of a jar into a walk to a bank, setting the jar on the shelf by the wall at home.}
\CRday{Day 43}{Ilmen 14, Y.H. 813 (Fourthday)  —  the Cross, the river road and the Weir, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  Preparations for the Fish Blessing went upriver with eels salted and traps lifted and Orra’s knot-accounts kept in the Eel House, a woman with green at one corner of her mouth looked at pots across the market and was gone unnamed, Orra Weir came onstage rope-handed and eel-scarred telling of a collector’s boat with four oars and giving a date where an answer should stand, Alda touched her unopened tin beside her and neither spoke of the third day, the Ilm ran higher under a thinning skin called weather, and the weak board in the plank walk and the Singing Sill’s early note were filed as gaps in a sixth room.}
\CRday{Day 44}{Ilmen 15, Y.H. 813 (Fifthday)  —  the Weir, the Eel House and the blessing stone, and the Vail kiln-house at dusk, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath  —  The hearth-maids blessed the traps on the flat stone while the eels ran as they always ran, Orra tied a forty-first knot she could not account for over the story of a small warm covered bundle with a flower carried up the Clay Yard in the year of the flower and said the word forty low into the basket and watched, while the forty-four-day-old boy kept the shape of the knot and the word on separate trays with Mira’s two cords still unread, the traps came up full, the river rose under its thinning skin and was called weather, and at dusk he was carried home with both crusts still in the fold and the fire behind him keeping four, four and a gap.}
